title: ECE Notes
text:
These notes accompany the Equivariant Covariance Estimator (ECE) project. The goal is to estimate and test for contemporaneous correlation between two time series in the presence of unknown mean shifts, without requiring explicit changepoint detection.
The notes combine theoretical derivations with R computations that verify the theory.

title: 2  Model Assumptions
text:
2.1 Error Structure
We observe input data sequences \(X = (X_1, \ldots, X_n)\) and \(Y = (Y_1, \ldots, Y_n)\). Each observation decomposes into a mean component and an error component:
\[
X_i = \theta_{x,i} + \varepsilon_{x,i}, \qquad Y_i = \theta_{y,i} + \varepsilon_{y,i}.
\]
The error terms \((\varepsilon_{x,i}, \varepsilon_{y,i})\) have zero mean and covariance matrix
\[
\Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma_x^2 & \sigma_{xy} \\ \sigma_{xy} & \sigma_y^2 \end{bmatrix}.
\]
We assume there is no autocorrelation: for \(i \neq j\),
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_{x,i}, \varepsilon_{x,j})
= \operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_{y,i}, \varepsilon_{y,j})
= \operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_{x,i}, \varepsilon_{y,j})
= 0.
\]
Contemporaneous dependence between \(X\) and \(Y\) is captured by \(\sigma_{xy} = \operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_{x,i}, \varepsilon_{y,i})\), the main quantity of interest in these notes.

title: 2  Model Assumptions
text:
2.2 Mean Structure
The mean components \(\theta_x = (\theta_{x,1}, \ldots, \theta_{x,n})\) and \(\theta_y = (\theta_{y,1}, \ldots, \theta_{y,n})\) are assumed to be piecewise constant. We call index \(i\) a change point when \(\theta_i \neq \theta_{i+1}\), and collect all change points in \(\tau = (\tau_1, \ldots, \tau_J)\) in ascending order. With \(\tau_0 = 0\) and \(\tau_{J+1} = n\), the shortest segment length is
\[
\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \min_{0 \le j \le J} \{\tau_{j+1} - \tau_j\}, \qquad \Theta_L = \{\theta : \mathcal{L}(\theta) \ge L\}.
\]
This allows frequent mean shifts while ensuring a minimum spacing \(L\) between consecutive change points.

title: 3  Lagged Differences
text:
3.1 \(k\)-Lagged Estimator
Using circular indexing \(i := [(i-1) \bmod n] + 1\), define the \(k\)-lagged cross-product sum
\[
T_k(X, Y) = \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - X_{i+k})(Y_i - Y_{i+k}).
\]
We abbreviate \(T_k(X) := T_k(X,X)\) and similarly for \(Y\).

title: 3  Lagged Differences
text:
3.2 Circular Version
A practical issue with \(T_k\) is that the number of terms \(n - k\) shrinks as \(k\) grows, making comparisons across lags unequal. To fix this, we embed the index set on a circle by redefining
\[
i \;:=\; [(i - 1) \bmod n] + 1,
\]
so that index \(n+1\) wraps back to \(1\). Under this convention every lag uses exactly \(n\) differences. The circular \(k\)-lagged covariance estimator is
\[
\hat{\sigma}_k(X, Y) = \frac{1}{2n}\, T_k(X, Y).
\]
Like the non-circular version, \(\hat{\sigma}_k\) is unbiased for \(\sigma_{xy}\) whenever \(1 \le k < n\) and there are no mean shifts. It is slightly more efficient because it uses all \(n\) differences at every lag.

title: 3  Lagged Differences
text:
3.3 Bias Under Mean Shifts
When mean shifts are present the estimator is no longer unbiased. To see why, expand a single lagged difference:
\[
X_i - X_{i+k} = (\theta_{x,i} - \theta_{x,i+k}) + (\varepsilon_{x,i} - \varepsilon_{x,i+k}).
\]
Whenever \(i\) and \(i+k\) straddle a change point, the mean difference \(\theta_{x,i} - \theta_{x,i+k}\) is nonzero and contaminates the cross-product. The resulting bias in \(T_k\) is
\[
\mathbb{E}[T_k(X, Y)] = 2n\sigma_{xy} + k\,\omega_{xy},
\qquad \omega_{xy} = T_1(\theta_x, \theta_y),
\]
so the bias of \(\hat{\sigma}_k\) grows linearly in \(k\).

title: 3  Lagged Differences
text:
3.4 Equivariant Covariance Estimator (ECE)
Since \(\mathbb{E}[T_k(X,Y)/2n] = \sigma_{xy} + k\,\omega_{xy}/2n\), the quantity \(\sigma_{xy}\) is the intercept of a line in \(k\). Fitting this line at \(k=1,2\) and extracting the intercept gives the ECE:
\[
\hat{\sigma}_{xy} = \frac{1}{2n}\bigl(2T_1(X,Y) - T_2(X,Y)\bigr).
\]
By linearity of expectation, \(\mathbb{E}[\hat{\sigma}_{xy}] = \sigma_{xy}\), so ECE is unbiased under the piecewise-constant mean model.

title: 4  Bilinear Form
text:
4.1 Solving for \(A\)
Definition. An estimator \(\tilde{s}(X, Y) = X^T A Y\) for \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\) is called bilinear.
Expanding using \(X = \theta_x + \varepsilon_x\) and \(Y = \theta_y + \varepsilon_y\) and taking expectations gives
\[
\mathbb{E}[\tilde{s}(X, Y)] = \theta_x^T A \theta_y + \operatorname{tr}(A)\, \sigma_{xy}.
\]
For unbiasedness, \(A\) must satisfy
To reduce the search space, we impose a symmetry condition. Let \(C_k\) be the circulant shift matrix, which shifts a vector \(k\) positions to the right circularly.
Definition. A bilinear estimator is equivariant if \(\tilde{s}(C_k X, C_k Y) = \tilde{s}(X, Y)\) for all \(k\).
Lemma (Equivariant \(\Leftrightarrow\) Symmetric Circulant). Since \(\tilde{s}\) is a covariance estimator, \(A\) must be symmetric. The bilinear estimator \(X^T A Y\) is equivariant if and only if \(A\) is a symmetric circulant: \[
A = \operatorname{circ}(a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor}, \ldots, a_1) = \begin{bmatrix}
a_0    & a_1    & \cdots & a_1    \\
a_1    & a_0    & \cdots & \vdots \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
a_1    & \cdots & a_1    & a_0
\end{bmatrix},
\] where \(a_k = a_{n-k}\) for all \(k\).
Proof. Since \(\tilde{s}(C_k X, C_k Y) = X^T(C_k^T A C_k)Y\), equivariance holds iff \(A = C_k^T A C_k\) for all \(k\), which is equivalent to \(A\) being circulant. Symmetry of \(A\) further requires \(a_k = a_{n-k}\), so \(A\) is a symmetric circulant. \(\square\)
This reduces the \(n^2\) free parameters of \(A\) to the \(n\) entries of its first row. Applying the unbiasedness constraints then uniquely determines \(A\), and the resulting estimator is exactly \(\hat{\sigma}_{xy}\).
Since \(A\) is a symmetric circulant, it is determined by \((a_0, \ldots, a_{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor})\). The unbiasedness conditions reduce to a linear system in these entries.
For a circulant \(A\), the condition \(\theta_x^T A \theta_y = 0\) for all piecewise-constant \(\theta_x, \theta_y \in \Theta_L\) is equivalent to requiring that the sum of all entries of every \(\ell \times \ell\) contiguous submatrix of \(A\) is zero, for \(\ell = L, \ldots, \lfloor n/2 \rfloor\). Denoting by \(A_\ell\) such a submatrix, this reads
\[
\|A_\ell\|_1 = 0, \qquad \ell = L, \ldots, \lfloor n/2 \rfloor.
\]
For a symmetric circulant, this sum depends only on \((a_0, \ldots, a_{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor})\) and takes the explicit form
\[
g(\ell) = \ell\, a_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{\min\{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor,\, \ell\}} 2(\ell - i)\, a_i + \sum_{i=\lfloor n/2 \rfloor + 1}^{\ell} 2(\ell - i)\, a_{n-i}.
\]
For \(L = 2\), setting \(g(\ell) = 0\) for \(\ell = 2, 3\) and using \(a_0 = 1/n\) gives
\[
g(2) = 2a_0 + 2a_1 = 0 \implies a_1 = -a_0,
\] \[
g(3) = 3a_0 + 4a_1 + 2a_2 = 0 \implies a_2 = \tfrac{a_0}{2},
\]
and for \(\ell \geq 4\) one shows by induction that \(a_{\ell - 1} = 0\). Together with \(a_0 = 1/n\), this uniquely determines \(A\).

title: 4  Bilinear Form
text:
4.2 Matrix Form of ECE
Proposition. For \(L = 2\), the ECE \(\hat{\sigma}_{xy} = X^T A Y\) where \(A = \frac{1}{n}\operatorname{circ}(a)\) and
\[
a = \left(1,\; -1,\; \tfrac{1}{2},\; 0,\; \ldots,\; 0,\; \tfrac{1}{2},\; -1\right).
\]
Proof. Since \(T_k(X,Y) = ((I-C_k)X)^T((I-C_k)Y)\), we have \(T_k(X,Y) = X^T A_k Y\) where
\[
A_k = (I - C_k)^T(I - C_k) = 2I - C_k - C_k^T.
\]
Since \(C_k = \operatorname{circ}(e_k)\), we have \(A_k = \operatorname{circ}(\tilde{a}_k)\) where the first row \(\tilde{a}_k\) has \(+2\) at position \(0\), \(-1\) at position \(k\), \(-1\) at position \(n-k\), and \(0\) elsewhere.
Substituting into \(\hat{\sigma}_{xy} = \frac{1}{2n}(2T_1 - T_2)\),
\[
A = \frac{1}{2n}(2A_1 - A_2) = \frac{1}{2n}\bigl(2(2I - C_1 - C_1^T) - (2I - C_2 - C_2^T)\bigr) = \frac{1}{n}\operatorname{circ}(a). \quad\square
\]

title: 4  Bilinear Form
text:
4.3 Derivation of \(\mathbb{E}[X^T A Y]\)
Substituting \(X = \theta_x + \varepsilon_x\) and \(Y = \theta_y + \varepsilon_y\),
\[
X^T A Y = (\theta_x + \varepsilon_x)^T A (\theta_y + \varepsilon_y)
= \theta_x^T A \theta_y + \theta_x^T A \varepsilon_y + \varepsilon_x^T A \theta_y + \varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y.
\]
Taking expectations and using \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_x] = \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_y] = 0\),
\[
\mathbb{E}[X^T A Y] = \theta_x^T A \theta_y + \theta_x^T A \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_y] + \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_x]^T A \theta_y + \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y]
= \theta_x^T A \theta_y + \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y].
\]
For the remaining term, since \(\varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y\) is a scalar,
\[
\varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y = \operatorname{tr}(\varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y).
\]
By the cyclic property of trace, \(\operatorname{tr}(\varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y) = \operatorname{tr}(A \varepsilon_y \varepsilon_x^T)\). Taking the expectation and applying linearity,
\[
\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y] = \operatorname{tr}(A\, \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_y \varepsilon_x^T]) = \operatorname{tr}(A \cdot \sigma_{xy} I) = \sigma_{xy}\operatorname{tr}(A),
\]
where we used \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_y \varepsilon_x^T] = \sigma_{xy} I\).
Therefore,
\[
\mathbb{E}[X^T A Y] = \theta_x^T A \theta_y + \sigma_{xy}\operatorname{tr}(A). \qquad \square
\]

title: 4  Bilinear Form
text:
4.4 Derivation of \(\operatorname{Var}(X^T A Y)\)
Using the same decomposition, write \(X^T A Y = \theta_x^T A \theta_y + \theta_x^T A \varepsilon_y + \varepsilon_x^T A \theta_y + \varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y\). Since the first term is a constant, it does not contribute to the variance, so
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X^T A Y) = \operatorname{Var}(\theta_x^T A \varepsilon_y + \varepsilon_x^T A \theta_y + \varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y).
\]
Expanding,
\[\begin{align*}
\operatorname{Var}(X^T A Y) &= \operatorname{Var}(\theta_x^T A \varepsilon_y) + \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_x^T A \theta_y) + \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y) \\
&\quad + 2\operatorname{Cov}(\theta_x^T A \varepsilon_y,\, \varepsilon_x^T A \theta_y) \\
&\quad + 2\operatorname{Cov}(\theta_x^T A \varepsilon_y,\, \varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y) \\
&\quad + 2\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_x^T A \theta_y,\, \varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y).
\end{align*}\]






Derivation of each term





Term 1: \(\operatorname{Var}(\theta_x^T A \varepsilon_y)\). Since \(\theta_x^T A\) is a fixed row vector, this is the variance of a linear form in \(\varepsilon_y\):
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\theta_x^T A \varepsilon_y) = \theta_x^T A \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_y) A^T \theta_x = \sigma_y^2\, \theta_x^T A A^T \theta_x = \sigma_y^2\, \theta_x^T A^2 \theta_x,
\]
where the last equality uses symmetry of \(A\).
Term 2: \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_x^T A \theta_y)\). By the same argument, \(A \theta_y\) is a fixed vector, so
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_x^T A \theta_y) = \theta_y^T A^T \operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_x) A \theta_y = \sigma_x^2\, \theta_y^T A^2 \theta_y.
\]
Term 3: \(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y)\). Apply the eigendecomposition \(A = Q\Lambda Q^T\) and let \(z_x = Q^T \varepsilon_x / \sigma_x\), \(z_y = Q^T \varepsilon_y / \sigma_y\), so that \(z_x, z_y \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\) with \(\operatorname{Cov}(z_x, z_y) = \rho I\) where \(\rho = \sigma_{xy}/(\sigma_x \sigma_y)\). Applying the eigendecomposition,
\[
\varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y = \sigma_x \sigma_y\, z_x^T \Lambda z_y = \sigma_x \sigma_y \sum_i \lambda_i z_{x,i} z_{y,i}.
\]
Since \(\operatorname{Cov}(z_x, z_y) = \rho I\) is diagonal, the pairs \((z_{x,i}, z_{y,i})\) are independent across \(i\), so
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y) = \sigma_x^2 \sigma_y^2 \sum_i \lambda_i^2\, \operatorname{Var}(z_{x,i} z_{y,i}).
\]
For each \(i\), \((z_{x,i}, z_{y,i})\) is a standard bivariate Gaussian with correlation \(\rho\), so \(\operatorname{Var}(z_{x,i} z_{y,i}) = 1 + \rho^2\) (see Appendix). Therefore,
\[
\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y) = \sigma_x^2 \sigma_y^2 (1 + \rho^2)\operatorname{tr}(A^2) = (\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + \sigma_{xy}^2)\operatorname{tr}(A^2).
\]
Term 4: \(\operatorname{Cov}(\theta_x^T A \varepsilon_y,\, \varepsilon_x^T A \theta_y)\). Since \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_x] = \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_y] = 0\), both terms have zero expectation, so the covariance reduces to
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(\theta_x^T A \varepsilon_y,\, \varepsilon_x^T A \theta_y) = \mathbb{E}[(\theta_x^T A \varepsilon_y)(\varepsilon_x^T A \theta_y)] = \theta_x^T A\, \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_y \varepsilon_x^T]\, A^T \theta_y = \sigma_{xy}\, \theta_x^T A^2 \theta_y,
\]
where we used \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_y \varepsilon_x^T] = \sigma_{xy} I\) and symmetry of \(A\).
Terms 5 and 6: \(\operatorname{Cov}(\theta_x^T A \varepsilon_y,\, \varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y)\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_x^T A \theta_y,\, \varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y)\). Since all terms have zero expectation, both covariances reduce to expectations of products involving one linear and one bilinear form in \((\varepsilon_x, \varepsilon_y)\). These are third-order moments of the zero-mean jointly Gaussian vector \((\varepsilon_x, \varepsilon_y)\), and all odd-order moments of a zero-mean Gaussian vanish. Therefore,
\[
\operatorname{Cov}(\theta_x^T A \varepsilon_y,\, \varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y) = 0, \qquad \operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_x^T A \theta_y,\, \varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y) = 0.
\]



Collecting all terms,
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X^T A Y) = \sigma_y^2\, \theta_x^T A^2 \theta_x + \sigma_x^2\, \theta_y^T A^2 \theta_y + 2\sigma_{xy}\, \theta_x^T A^2 \theta_y + (\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + \sigma_{xy}^2)\operatorname{tr}(A^2).
\]
The noise contribution \((\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + \sigma_{xy}^2)\operatorname{tr}(A^2) = O(1/n)\) by the lower bound on \(\operatorname{tr}(A^2)\) (see Appendix B), which shows the estimator is consistent.

title: 4  Bilinear Form
text:
4.5 Solving for \(A\) (\(L > 2\))
For \(L > 2\), the unbiasedness constraints leave a multi-dimensional solution space for \(a\), so we have freedom to optimize. The full variance is
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X^T A Y) = \sigma_y^2\, \theta_x^T A^2 \theta_x + \sigma_x^2\, \theta_y^T A^2 \theta_y + 2\sigma_{xy}\, \theta_x^T A^2 \theta_y + (\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + \sigma_{xy}^2)\operatorname{tr}(A^2).
\]
Since \(\theta_x\) and \(\theta_y\) are unknown, the signal-dependent terms cannot be minimized directly. The only term we can control is the noise term \((\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + \sigma_{xy}^2)\operatorname{tr}(A^2)\), which for fixed noise levels reduces to minimizing \(\operatorname{tr}(A^2)\). This gives the optimization problem
\[
\min_{a \in \mathbb{R}^n} \operatorname{tr}(A^2) \quad \text{subject to} \quad \|A_\ell\|_1 = 0,\ \ell = L, \ldots, \lfloor n/2 \rfloor, n, \quad \operatorname{tr}(A) = 1,
\]
where \(A = \operatorname{circ}(a)\).
Reducing to a norm minimization. Since \(A = \operatorname{circ}(a)\) is a circulant, every row of \(A\) is a cyclic permutation of \(a\) and therefore has the same squared norm \(\|a\|^2\). The Frobenius norm of \(A\) is thus
\[
\|A\|_F^2 = n\|a\|^2.
\]
Since \(A\) is symmetric, \(\operatorname{tr}(A^2) = \operatorname{tr}(A^T A) = \|A\|_F^2 = n\|a\|^2\). Minimizing \(\operatorname{tr}(A^2)\) is therefore equivalent to minimizing \(\|a\|^2\). Because the unbiasedness constraints are linear in \(a\), the problem reduces to
\[
\min_{a \in \mathbb{R}^n} \|a\|^2 \quad \text{subject to} \quad \|A_\ell\|_1 = 0,\ \ell = L, \ldots, \lfloor n/2 \rfloor, n, \quad \operatorname{tr}(A) = 1,
\]
where \(A = \operatorname{circ}(a)\). Both sets of constraints are linear in \(a\), so this is a quadratic program with a unique solution — the minimum-norm point in the feasible affine subspace.

title: 4  Bilinear Form
text:
4.6 Regression Approach
A natural way to estimate \(\sigma_{xy}\) is to exploit the linear relationship \(\mathbb{E}[T_k(X,Y)] = 2n\sigma_{xy} + k\,\omega_{xy}\) (established in the Lagged Differences chapter). Stacking \(k = 1, \ldots, L\) gives a linear model
\[
\mathbb{E}[R] = K\beta,
\qquad
K = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ 1 & L \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times 2},
\quad
\beta = \begin{pmatrix} 2n\sigma_{xy} \\ \omega_{xy} \end{pmatrix},
\]
where \(R_k = T_k(X,Y)\). The OLS estimate is \(\hat\beta = (K^TK)^{-1}K^T R\), and the regression estimator of \(\sigma_{xy}\) is its first component rescaled:
\[
\tilde\sigma_{xy} = \frac{1}{2n}\, e_1^T(K^TK)^{-1}K^T R = \sum_{k=1}^L c_k R_k,
\]
where \(c_k = \frac{1}{2n}\bigl[(K^TK)^{-1}K^T\bigr]_{1k}\) are the coefficients from the first row of \(\frac{1}{2n}(K^TK)^{-1}K^T\).
Relationship \(T_k(X,Y) = X^T A_k Y\). Since
\[
T_k(X,Y) = \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - X_{i+k})(Y_i - Y_{i+k}) = \bigl((I - C_k)X\bigr)^T\bigl((I - C_k)Y\bigr),
\]
we have \(T_k(X,Y) = X^T A_k Y\) with
\[
A_k = (I - C_k)^T(I - C_k) = 2I - C_k - C_k^T.
\]
Substituting \(R_k = X^T A_k Y\) into the regression estimator,
\[
\tilde\sigma_{xy} = \sum_{k=1}^L c_k R_k = X^T A Y,
\]
so the regression estimator is a bilinear form \(X^T A Y\) with
\[
A = \sum_{k=1}^L c_k\, A_k.
\]
Since each \(A_k = 2I - C_k - C_k^T\) is a symmetric circulant, \(A\) is also a symmetric circulant, determined by its first row \(\tilde{a} \in \mathbb{R}^n\).
First row of the regression matrix. Writing \(A_k = \operatorname{circ}(a_k)\) where \(a_k\) denotes the first row of \(A_k\), linearity of the circulant map gives
\[
A = \operatorname{circ}(\tilde{a}), \qquad \tilde{a} = \sum_{k=1}^L c_k\, a_k.
\]
From \(A_k = 2I - C_k - C_k^T\) and the circulant form of \(C_k\) (see Mathematical Background), the first row is \(a_k = 2e_0 - e_k - e_{n-k}\), where \(e_j\) denotes the \(j\)-th standard basis vector.

title: 4  Bilinear Form
text:
4.7 Feasibility of the Regression Estimator
To show that \(\tilde{a}\) is the minimum-norm solution, we must verify it is feasible, i.e., that it satisfies the trace and unbiasedness constraints.
The regression estimator is the bilinear form \(X^T A Y\) with \(A = \sum_{k=1}^L c_k A_k\), where \(c_k = H_{1,k} = \frac{2L+1-3k}{nL(L-1)}\). Since we evaluate \(g(\ell)\) only for \(\ell \geq L\), every \(k \leq L\) satisfies \(k \leq \ell\), so the Lemma (see Other Mathematical Results) gives \(\mathbf{1}_\ell^T A_k \mathbf{1}_\ell = 2k\). By linearity, \[g(\ell) = \mathbf{1}_\ell^T A\, \mathbf{1}_\ell = 2\sum_{k=1}^L c_k k,\] which is independent of \(\ell\). Both constraints then reduce to evaluating \(\sum_k c_k\) and \(\sum_k c_k k\) via the closed form of \(c_k\).
Trace constraint: \(\operatorname{tr}(A) = 1\). Since \(\operatorname{tr}(A_k) = \operatorname{tr}(2I - C_k - C_k^T) = 2n\) (as \(C_k\) has no fixed points for \(k \geq 1\)), we have \(\operatorname{tr}(A) = 2n\sum_k c_k\). Applying the Gaussian sum \(\sum_{k=1}^L k = \frac{L(L+1)}{2}\), \[\sum_{k=1}^L c_k = \frac{1}{nL(L-1)}\left[(2L+1)L - \frac{3L(L+1)}{2}\right] = \frac{1}{n(L-1)}\cdot\frac{L-1}{2} = \frac{1}{2n}.\] Therefore \(\operatorname{tr}(A) = 2n \cdot \frac{1}{2n} = 1\). \(\square\)
Unbiasedness: \(g(\ell) = 0\) for \(\ell = L, \ldots, \lfloor n/2 \rfloor\). For \(\ell \geq L\), \(g(\ell) = 2\sum_k c_k k\). Applying the Gaussian sums \(\sum_{k=1}^L k = \frac{L(L+1)}{2}\) and \(\sum_{k=1}^L k^2 = \frac{L(L+1)(2L+1)}{6}\), \[\sum_{k=1}^L c_k k = \frac{1}{nL(L-1)}\left[(2L+1)\frac{L(L+1)}{2} - \frac{3L(L+1)(2L+1)}{6}\right] = \frac{(2L+1)L(L+1)}{nL(L-1)}\left[\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2}\right] = 0.\] Therefore \(g(\ell) = 0\) for all \(\ell \geq L\). \(\square\)

title: 4  Bilinear Form
section: 4.8 The Regression Estimator is the Minimum-Norm Estimator
text:
4.8 The Regression Estimator is the Minimum-Norm Estimator
Having established feasibility, it remains to show that \(\tilde{a}\) is the minimum-norm feasible solution.
Setup. Since the unbiasedness constraints are homogeneous (\(Ga = 0\)), every feasible \(a\) lies in \(\mathrm{null}(G)\). The trace constraint \(\mathrm{tr}(A) = 1\) is the only inhomogeneous condition, cutting out an affine hyperplane within \(\mathrm{null}(G)\): \[F = \{a \in \mathrm{null}(G) : \mathrm{tr}(A) = 1\}.\] Let \(a^* \in F\) be the minimum-norm feasible solution. We will show \(a^* = \tilde{a}\) by writing \(a^* = \tilde{a} + w\) with \(w = a^* - \tilde{a}\) and expanding: \[\|a^*\|^2 = \|\tilde{a}\|^2 + \|w\|^2 + 2\langle\tilde{a}, w\rangle.\] Steps 1 and 2 below show \(\langle\tilde{a}, w\rangle = 0\), so the expansion reduces to \[\|a^*\|^2 = \|\tilde{a}\|^2 + \|w\|^2.\] Since \(a^*\) is optimal and \(\tilde{a}\) is feasible, \(\|a^*\|^2 \leq \|\tilde{a}\|^2\), so \[\|a^*\|^2 = \|\tilde{a}\|^2 + \|w\|^2 \leq \|\tilde{a}\|^2 \implies \|w\|^2 \leq 0.\] Therefore \(w = 0\) and \(a^* = \tilde{a}\).
Step 1: Characterize vectors satisfying \((*)\).
Since both \(a^*, \tilde{a} \in F\), the difference \(w = a^* - \tilde{a}\) satisfies \(Gw = 0\) (as both \(Ga^* = 0\) and \(G\tilde{a} = 0\)) and \(\mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{circ}(w)) = \mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{circ}(a^*)) - \mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{circ}(\tilde{a})) = 1 - 1 = 0\). Since \(\mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{circ}(w)) = nw_0\), we have \(w_0 = 0\). So \(w\) satisfies \[Gw = 0, \quad w_0 = 0. \tag{$*$}\]
Let \(w\) satisfy \((*)\). The constraint matrix \(G\) has entries \(G_{\ell,0} = \ell\) and \(G_{\ell,k} = 2(\ell-k)^+\) for \(k \geq 1\), so \(Gw = 0\) requires for each \(\ell = L, \ldots, \lfloor n/2 \rfloor\):
\[\ell\, w_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor} 2(\ell - k)^+\, w_k = 0.\]
We analyze this system by applying a first-difference operator twice. For any matrix \(B\) with \(r\) rows, define \(M(B)\) as the \((r-1) \times r\) bidiagonal matrix applied to \(B\):
\[M(B) = \begin{pmatrix} -1 & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & & \ddots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & 0 & \cdots & -1 & 1 \end{pmatrix} B,\]
so that \(M(B)_\ell = B_{\ell+1} - B_\ell\). We write \(M^2G\) as shorthand for \(M(M(G))\) — applying the operator twice sequentially, each time with a smaller matrix of appropriate dimensions. Since \(Gw = 0\) implies \(M(G)w = 0\) and \(M(M(G))w = 0\), each application yields simpler conditions.
Step 1a: Show \(w_k = 0\) for \(k > L\).
First application (\(M(G)w = 0\)). Subtracting the \(\ell\)-th row from the \((\ell+1)\)-th gives
\[w_0 + 2\sum_{k=1}^{\ell} w_k = 0, \qquad \ell = L, \ldots, \lfloor n/2 \rfloor - 1.\]
The resulting matrix \(MG\) has a column of \(1\)s in position \(k=0\) and \(2\)s in positions \(k = 1, \ldots, \ell\) (filling in one more entry per row):
\[MG = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & \cdots & 2 & 0 & 0 & \cdots \\ 1 & 2 & \cdots & 2 & 2 & 0 & \cdots \\ 1 & 2 & \cdots & 2 & 2 & 2 & \cdots \\ \vdots & & & & & & \ddots \end{pmatrix}.\]
Second application (\(M(M(G))w = 0\)). Subtracting consecutive equations from \(M(G)w = 0\) gives \(2w_{\ell+1} = 0\) for each \(\ell = L, \ldots, \lfloor n/2 \rfloor - 2\), so \(w_k = 0\) for all \(k > L\).
The matrix \(M(M(G))\) has exactly one nonzero entry per row — a \(2\) in column \(\ell + 1\) — making the zero conditions on each \(w_k\) explicit:
\[M(M(G)) = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & \cdots & 0 & 2 & 0 & 0 & \cdots \\ 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 & 2 & 0 & \cdots \\ 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 & 0 & 2 & \cdots \\ \vdots & & & & & & \ddots \end{pmatrix}.\]
Step 1b: Characterize \((w_1, \ldots, w_L)\).
Having zeroed out \(w_k\) for \(k > L\), we need two conditions on the remaining entries \((w_1, \ldots, w_L)\). We obtain these by working back through \(MGw = 0\) and \(Gw = 0\) at \(\ell = L\) — each provides one independent condition, and no further applications of \(M\) are needed to characterize the null space.
Recall from Step 1a that \(M(G)w = 0\) gives \[w_0 + 2\sum_{k=1}^{\ell} w_k = 0, \qquad \ell = L, \ldots, \lfloor n/2 \rfloor - 1.\] Setting \(\ell = L\) and substituting \(w_k = 0\) for \(k > L\) gives \(w_0 + 2\sum_{k=1}^L w_k = 0\). Since \(w_0 = 0\) by \((*)\), this forces \(\sum_{k=1}^L w_k = 0\).
Similarly, recall from Step 1a that \(Gw = 0\) gives \(\ell\, w_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor} 2(\ell-k)^+\, w_k = 0\). Setting \(\ell = L\) and splitting the sum: \[L\, w_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{L} 2(L-k)^+\, w_k + \sum_{k=L+1}^{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor} 2(L-k)^+\, w_k = 0.\] The second sum vanishes since \((L-k)^+ = 0\) for \(k > L\), and \(w_0 = 0\) by \((*)\), leaving \(\sum_{k=1}^L 2(L-k)\, w_k = 0\). Expanding and applying \(\sum_{k=1}^L w_k = 0\) gives \(\sum_{k=1}^L k\, w_k = 0\).
Therefore the vectors satisfying \((*)\) are exactly those with \(w_0 = 0\), \(w_k = 0\) for \(k > L\), and \((w_1, \ldots, w_L)\) satisfying
\[\sum_{k=1}^L w_k = 0, \qquad \sum_{k=1}^L k\,w_k = 0.\]
To summarize, each level of differentiation contributes one layer of structure:



Equation
Conclusion




\(M(M(G))w = 0\)

\(M(G)w = 0\) at \(\ell = L\)

Step 2: Show \(\tilde{a} \perp w\).
Since \(\tilde{a} = \sum_{k=1}^L c_k \tilde{a}_k\), by linearity of the inner product: \[\langle \tilde{a}, w \rangle = \sum_{k=1}^L c_k \langle \tilde{a}_k, w \rangle.\]
Since \(\tilde{a}_k = 2e_0 - e_k - e_{n-k}\), \[\langle \tilde{a}_k, w \rangle = 2w_0 - w_k - w_{n-k}.\]
From Step 1: \(w_0 = 0\), and for \(k \in \{1, \ldots, L\}\) we have \(n - k > L\), so \(w_{n-k} = 0\). Therefore \(\langle \tilde{a}_k, w \rangle = -w_k\), and \[\langle \tilde{a}, w \rangle = -\sum_{k=1}^L c_k\, w_k.\]
Since \(c_k = \frac{2L+1-3k}{nL(L-1)}\) is affine in \(k\),
\[\sum_{k=1}^L c_k\, w_k = \frac{2L+1}{nL(L-1)} \sum_{k=1}^L w_k - \frac{3}{nL(L-1)} \sum_{k=1}^L k\,w_k = 0,\]
where both sums vanish by Step 1. Therefore \(\langle \tilde{a}, w \rangle = 0\) for all \(w\) satisfying \((*)\). \(\square\)

title: 5  Kappa Estimation
text:
5.1 Motivation
The asymptotic variance of \(\hat\rho\) is \[
v^2 = \frac{1}{n}\!\left[(1-\rho^2)\!\left(\omega_x^2 + \omega_y^2 - 2\rho\,\omega_{xy}\right) + \frac{\rho^2}{4}(\kappa_{40}+2\kappa_{22}+\kappa_{04}) - \rho(\kappa_{31}+\kappa_{13}) + \tfrac{5}{2}(1-\rho^2)^2 + \kappa_{22}\right].
\] Under \(H_0: \rho = 0\) this reduces to \[
\boxed{
v^2 = \frac{1}{n}\!\left(\omega_x^2 + \omega_y^2 + \kappa_{22} + \frac{5}{2}\right).
}
\] Under Gaussianity \(\kappa_{22} = 1\) and the null variance is \((\omega_x^2 + \omega_y^2 + 7/2)/n\). Without Gaussianity, \(\kappa_{22}\) is unknown and must be estimated from data to form a valid test statistic.

title: 5  Kappa Estimation
text:
5.2 Estimating \(\kappa_{22}\)
There are multiple strategies to estimate \(\kappa_{22}\). Let \(s_i^{(k)} = (X_i - X_{i+k})(Y_i - Y_{i+k})\) and \[
S_{xy,i} = \frac{s_i^{(1)} + s_{i+1}^{(1)} - s_i^{(2)}}{2},
\] so that \(E[S_{xy,i}] = \sigma_{xy}\) at every index regardless of change points. Replacing \(Y\) with \(X\) gives \(S_{xx,i}\) (with \(E[S_{xx,i}] = \sigma_x^2\)), and similarly \(S_{yy,i}\) (with \(E[S_{yy,i}] = \sigma_y^2\)). Their averages satisfy \(\bar S_{xx} = \hat\sigma_x^2\), \(\bar S_{yy} = \hat\sigma_y^2\), \(\bar S_{xy} = \hat\sigma_{xy}\).

5.2.1 \(\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\sigma}_{xy})\)-Based Estimator
We find that \[
n\operatorname{Var}(\bar{S}_{xy}) = \kappa_{22}\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + \frac{3\sigma_{xy}^2 + 4\sigma_{xy}\omega_{xy}}{2} + \left(\frac{\omega_x^2}{\sigma_x^2} + \frac{\omega_y^2}{\sigma_y^2} + \frac{5}{2}\right)\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2.
\]
Solving for \(\kappa_{22}\) and plugging in estimates gives \[
\boxed{\hat\kappa_{22}^{(xy)} = \frac{n\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\bar{S}_{xy})}{\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_y^2} - \frac{3}{2}\frac{\hat\sigma_{xy}^2}{\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_y^2} - 2\frac{\hat\sigma_{xy}\hat\omega_{xy}}{\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_y^2} - \frac{\hat\omega_x^2}{\hat\sigma_x^2} - \frac{\hat\omega_y^2}{\hat\sigma_y^2} - \frac{5}{2}.}
\]


5.2.2 \(\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\sigma}_x^2, \hat{\sigma}_y^2)\)-Based Estimator
We find that \[
n\operatorname{Cov}(\bar{S}_{xx}, \bar{S}_{yy}) = (\kappa_{22} - 1)\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 2\sigma_{xy}^2 + 4\sigma_{xy}\omega_{xy}.
\]
Solving for \(\kappa_{22}\) and plugging in estimates gives \[
\boxed{\hat\kappa_{22}^{(xx,yy)} = \frac{n\widehat{\operatorname{Cov}}(\bar{S}_{xx}, \bar{S}_{yy})}{\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_y^2} - 2\frac{\hat\sigma_{xy}^2}{\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_y^2} - 4\frac{\hat\sigma_{xy}\hat\omega_{xy}}{\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_y^2} + 1.}
\]


5.2.3 Regression Estimator
Let us define \[
T_k^{(2)}(X, Y) = \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - X_{i+k})^2 (Y_i - Y_{i+k})^2.
\]
It follows that \[
\begin{aligned}
E[T_k^{(2)}(X, Y)]
&= 2n(\kappa_{22}-1)\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 8\sigma_{xy}T_k(\theta_x,\theta_y) + 4n\sigma_{xy}^2 \\
&\quad + T_k^{(2)}(\theta_x, \theta_y) + 2\sigma_y^2 T_k(\theta_x,\theta_x) + 2\sigma_x^2 T_k(\theta_y,\theta_y) + 4n\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
All \(\theta\)-dependent terms vanish in \(2E[T_1^{(2)}] - E[T_2^{(2)}]\), giving \[
2E[T_1^{(2)}(X,Y)] - E[T_2^{(2)}(X,Y)] = 2n(\kappa_{22}+1)\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 4n\sigma_{xy}^2.
\]
Solving for \(\kappa_{22}\) and plugging in estimates gives \[
\boxed{\hat\kappa_{22}^{r} = \frac{2T_1^{(2)}(X,Y) - T_2^{(2)}(X,Y)}{2n\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_y^2} - 2\frac{\hat\sigma_{xy}^2}{\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_y^2} - 1.}
\]


5.2.4 Method of Moments Estimator
This method is inspired from the classical approach.
The classical method to estimate \(\kappa_{22}\) is something like this \[
\hat{\kappa}_{22} = \frac{E(\varepsilon_x^2 \varepsilon_y^2)}{\sigma_x^2 \sigma_y^2}.
\]
Of course, we cannot directly access \(\varepsilon_x\) and \(\varepsilon_y\) in the presence of change points. Instead, we use a proxy:
\[
\hat{\kappa}_{22} = \frac{E(S_{xx} S_{yy}) }{\sigma_x^2 \sigma_y^2}.
\]
Unfortunately, it is not so simple. If we do some analysis, we’ll find that
\[
\frac{1}{n}\sum_i E[S_{xx,i}\,S_{yy,i}] = \kappa_{22}\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 3\sigma_{xy}^2 + 4\sigma_{xy}\omega_{xy}.
\]
Therefore, we propose the method of moments estimator: \[
\boxed{
  \hat{\kappa}_{22}^{\mathrm{MoM}} = \frac{\langle S_{xx}\,S_{yy}\rangle}{\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_y^2} - 3\frac{\hat\sigma_{xy}^2}{\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_y^2} - 4\frac{\hat\sigma_{xy}\hat\omega_{xy}}{\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_y^2}.
}
\]

title: 6  Z-Test
text:
6.1 Diagnostics
Define the lag-\(k\) cross-product statistic \(T_k(X, Y) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (X_i - X_{i+k})(Y_i - Y_{i+k})\), and let \[
Z = \begin{pmatrix} Z_1 \\ Z_2 \\ Z_3 \\ Z_4 \\ Z_5 \\ Z_6 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} T_1(X,X) \\ T_2(X,X) \\ T_1(Y,Y) \\ T_2(Y,Y) \\ T_1(X,Y) \\ T_2(X,Y) \end{pmatrix}.
\]
The proof applies the Multivariate Delta Method in three steps:
Step 1. Show that \[
\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}(Z - \mu_Z) \xrightarrow{d} N(\mathbf{0}, \Sigma_Z), \quad \mu_Z = \mathbb{E}[Z].
\]
Step 2. Compute \(\Sigma_Z = \mathrm{Cov}(Z)\).
Step 3. Define \[
g(Z) = \frac{2Z_5 - Z_6}{\sqrt{(2Z_1 - Z_2)(2Z_3 - Z_4)}} = \hat\rho.
\] Since \(g(\mu_Z) = \rho\), the multivariate delta method gives \[
\sqrt{n}(\hat\rho - \rho) \xrightarrow{d} N(0,\, v^2), \quad v^2 = \nabla g(\mu_Z)^\top \Sigma_Z\, \nabla g(\mu_Z).
\]
To verify the formulas, we simulate scenario 2 (\(n = 1000\), \(L = 4\), \(r = 0.3\)) under two error distributions and compare the empirical covariance matrix of \(Z\) to the theoretical \(\Sigma_Z\).
For each error type, we run 500 outer replicates. In each replicate, we draw 10 independent datasets, compute \(Z\) for each, and take their sample covariance as one estimate of \(\Sigma_Z\). Each panel in the grid below shows the distribution of residuals (estimated minus theoretical) for one entry of \(\Sigma_Z\) across the 500 replicates. The red line marks zero (no bias) and the orange line marks the sample mean. The p-value is from a one-sample t-test of whether the mean residual is zero.

title: 6  Z-Test
text:
Test: \(Var(\hat{\rho})\) is Scale-Invariant





We can define the asymptotic variance of \(\hat{\rho}\) as \[
v^2 = \frac{1}{n}\left[
(1-\rho^2)\!\left(\frac{\omega_x^2}{\sigma_x^2} + \frac{\omega_y^2}{\sigma_y^2} - \frac{2\rho\,\omega_{xy}}{\sigma_x\sigma_y}\right)
+ \frac{\rho^2}{4}(\kappa_{40} + 2\kappa_{22} + \kappa_{04})
- \rho(\kappa_{31} + \kappa_{13})
+ \kappa_{22} + \frac{5}{2}(1-\rho^2)^2
\right].
\]
Since \(\widehat\rho(aX, bY) = \widehat\rho(X, Y)\) for any \(a, b > 0\), the asymptotic variance \(v^2\) must be invariant under \(X \to aX\), \(Y \to bY\). We verify this term by term.
\(\omega\) terms. Scaling \(X\) by \(a\) sends \(\theta_x \to a\theta_x\), so \(\omega_x^2 \to a^2\omega_x^2\) and \(\sigma_x \to a\sigma_x\). Similarly \(\omega_y \to b\omega_y\), \(\omega_{xy} \to ab\,\omega_{xy}\). The ratios \[
\frac{\omega_x^2}{\sigma_x^2} \to \frac{a^2\omega_x^2}{a^2\sigma_x^2} = \frac{\omega_x^2}{\sigma_x^2}, \qquad
\frac{\rho\,\omega_{xy}}{\sigma_x\sigma_y} \to \frac{\rho\cdot ab\,\omega_{xy}}{a\sigma_x\cdot b\sigma_y} = \frac{\rho\,\omega_{xy}}{\sigma_x\sigma_y}
\] are unchanged.
\(\kappa\) terms. The \(\kappa_{rs}\) are cumulants of the standardized errors \(\varepsilon_x/\sigma_x\) and \(\varepsilon_y/\sigma_y\). Scaling \(X\) by \(a\) scales both \(\varepsilon_x\) and \(\sigma_x\) by \(a\), leaving the ratio unchanged, so all \(\kappa_{rs}\) are invariant. \(\rho\) is invariant by definition.
Therefore \(v^2\) is scale-invariant, and we may study \(X/\sigma_x\), \(Y/\sigma_y\) in place of \(X\), \(Y\) without loss of generality. Setting \(\sigma_x = \sigma_y = 1\):
\[
v^2 = \frac{1}{n}\left[
(1-\rho^2)\!\left(\omega_x^2 + \omega_y^2 - 2\rho\,\omega_{xy}\right)
+ \frac{\rho^2}{4}(\kappa_{40} + 2\kappa_{22} + \kappa_{04})
- \rho(\kappa_{31} + \kappa_{13})
+ \kappa_{22} + \frac{5}{2}(1-\rho^2)^2
\right].
\]

text:
6.2 Variance Difference: General vs. Gaussian
Recall the asymptotic variance under the general and Gaussian assumptions: \[
V = \frac{1}{n}\left[(1-\rho^2)\!\left(\frac{\omega_x^2}{\sigma_x^2} + \frac{\omega_y^2}{\sigma_y^2} - \frac{2\rho\,\omega_{xy}}{\sigma_x\sigma_y}\right) + \frac{\rho^2}{4}(\kappa_{40}+2\kappa_{22}+\kappa_{04}) - \rho(\kappa_{31}+\kappa_{13}) + \frac{5}{2}(1-\rho^2)^2 + \kappa_{22}\right],
\] \[
V_G = \frac{1}{n}(1-\rho^2)\!\left(\frac{\omega_x^2}{\sigma_x^2} + \frac{\omega_y^2}{\sigma_y^2} - \frac{2\rho\,\omega_{xy}}{\sigma_x\sigma_y} + \frac{7}{2}(1-\rho^2)\right).
\] The jump-noise terms cancel, giving \[
V - V_G = \frac{1}{n}\left[\frac{\rho^2}{4}(\kappa_{40}+2\kappa_{22}+\kappa_{04}) - \rho(\kappa_{31}+\kappa_{13}) + \kappa_{22} - (1-\rho^2)^2\right].
\] This is zero under the Gaussian assumption and measures the excess variance due to non-Gaussianity.

title: 7  Multiplier Bootstrap Test
text:
7.1 Notation
We test the hypotheses \[H_0: \Sigma = I_p \quad \text{vs} \quad H_1: \Sigma \neq I_p.\] Equivalently, this is a test of whether all off-diagonal entries \(\sigma_{xy} = 0\), which are precisely the quantities estimated by the ECE.
Outline. The Multiplier Bootstrap provides a distribution-free null distribution for a sum of mean-zero independent terms. The ECE satisfies neither condition directly: its summands are neither mean-zero nor independent. We address each in turn. First, we reparametrize the ECE as a sum of terms \(s_i^{(k)}\) that are mean-zero under \(H_0\). Second, we partition these terms into three subsequences, each comprising independent terms. Each subsequence yields a p-value via the Multiplier Bootstrap. Finally, since the three subsequences are mutually dependent, we combine their p-values using the Cauchy Combination Test.
Using circular indexing \(i := [(i-1) \bmod n] + 1\), define the \(k\)-lagged sum \[T_k(X, Y) = \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - X_{i+k})(Y_i - Y_{i+k}).\]
For notational convenience, define \(s_i^{(k)} = (X_i - X_{i+k})(Y_i - Y_{i+k})\), so that \[T_k(X,Y) = \sum_{i=1}^n s_i^{(k)}.\]

title: 7  Multiplier Bootstrap Test
text:
7.2 Multiplier Bootstrap
The Multiplier Bootstrap requires each summand to be mean-zero. The terms \(s_i^{(k)}\) do not satisfy this directly.
Making Terms Mean Zero.
Under circular indexing, shifting all indices by 1 leaves \(T_1\) unchanged: \[T_1(X,Y) = \sum_{i=1}^n s_i^{(1)} = \sum_{i=1}^n s_{i+1}^{(1)}.\] Therefore \(2T_1(X,Y) = \sum_{i=1}^n \left(s_i^{(1)} + s_{i+1}^{(1)}\right)\), and the ECE estimator becomes \[\hat\sigma_{xy} = \frac{2T_1(X,Y) - T_2(X,Y)}{2n} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \underbrace{\frac{s_i^{(1)} + s_{i+1}^{(1)} - s_i^{(2)}}{2}}_{S_i} = \bar{S}.\]






Proof: \(S_i\) is mean-zero under \(H_0\)





Define \(h_i^{(k)} = (\theta_{x,i} - \theta_{x,i+k})(\theta_{y,i} - \theta_{y,i+k})\) and \(e_i^{(k)} = (\varepsilon_{x,i} - \varepsilon_{x,i+k})(\varepsilon_{y,i} - \varepsilon_{y,i+k})\). Since cross terms have mean zero, \(\mathbb{E}[s_i^{(k)}] = h_i^{(k)} + 2\sigma_{xy}\). Therefore \[\mathbb{E}[S_i] = \tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(h_i^{(1)} + h_{i+1}^{(1)} - h_i^{(2)}\bigr) + \sigma_{xy}.\] Under \(H_0\) (\(\sigma_{xy} = 0\)), it remains to show \(h_i^{(1)} + h_{i+1}^{(1)} - h_i^{(2)} = 0\). We consider two cases.
If there is a change point at \(i\): minimum segment length 2 forces \(\theta_{i+1} = \theta_{i+2}\), so \(h_{i+1}^{(1)} = 0\) and \(h_i^{(2)} = h_i^{(1)}\). Hence \(h_i^{(1)} + 0 - h_i^{(1)} = 0\).
If there is a change point at \(i+1\): then \(\theta_i = \theta_{i+1}\), so \(h_i^{(1)} = 0\) and \(h_i^{(2)} = h_{i+1}^{(1)}\). Hence \(0 + h_{i+1}^{(1)} - h_{i+1}^{(1)} = 0\).
If there is no change point at either index, all terms are zero. Hence \(\mathbb{E}[S_i] = 0\) under \(H_0\).

Making Terms Independent.
Each \(S_i\) depends only on observations \(X_i, X_{i+1}, X_{i+2}\) (and the same for \(Y\)), so \(S_i\) and \(S_j\) are independent whenever \(|i - j| \geq 3\). This motivates partitioning by residue mod 3: \[\{S_1, S_4, S_7, \ldots\}, \quad \{S_2, S_5, S_8, \ldots\}, \quad \{S_3, S_6, S_9, \ldots\}.\] Within each subsequence, consecutive terms are at least 3 apart, so the terms are independent. However, the three subsequences share observations and are mutually dependent, so their p-values cannot be combined trivially.

title: 7  Multiplier Bootstrap Test
text:
7.3 Cauchy Combination Test
Given p-values \(p_1, p_2, p_3\) from the three subsequences, the CCT statistic is \[T = \sum_{j=1}^3 w_j \tan\!\left(\left(\tfrac{1}{2} - p_j\right)\pi\right),\] where \(w_j > 0\) are weights with \(\sum_j w_j = 1\), typically \(w_j = 1/3\). Under \(H_0\), each \(p_j\) is uniformly distributed on \([0,1]\), so each summand is standard Cauchy. The key property of the CCT is that \(T\) is approximately standard Cauchy under \(H_0\) regardless of the dependence structure among the \(p_j\). The combined p-value is the upper-tail probability \(p = 1 - F_{\mathrm{Cauchy}}(T)\), where \(F_{\mathrm{Cauchy}}(t) = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{\arctan(t)}{\pi}\) is the standard Cauchy CDF. Substituting, \[p = 1 - \frac{1}{2} - \frac{\arctan(T)}{\pi} = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{\arctan(T)}{\pi}.\]






Code: Combined P-value is Uniform Under \(H_0\)

title: 8  Parametric Bootstrap Test
text:
8.1 Parametric Bootstrap Test
Let \(S_i \in \mathbb{R}^{\binom{p}{2}}\) denote the vector of ECE terms across all pairs at index \(i\), so that \(\bar{S}_j = \hat\sigma_{x_j y_j}\) for each pair \(j\). To test \(H_0\), we need the variance of \(\bar{S} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n S_i\).
Since \(S_i\) depends only on observations at indices \(i, i+1, i+2\), terms separated by 3 or more indices are independent. The variance therefore has bandwidth 2: \[\begin{align*}
\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\bar{S}\right) &= \frac{1}{n^2}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n \operatorname{Var}(S_i) + \sum_{i=1}^n\bigl[\operatorname{Cov}(S_i, S_{i+1}) + \operatorname{Cov}(S_{i+1}, S_i)\bigr]\right. \\
&\quad\left. + \sum_{i=1}^n\bigl[\operatorname{Cov}(S_i, S_{i+2}) + \operatorname{Cov}(S_{i+2}, S_i)\bigr]\right).
\end{align*}\] Plugging in \(\operatorname{Var}(S_i) = \mathbb{E}[S_i S_i^\top]\) and \(\operatorname{Cov}(S_i, S_{i+k}) = \mathbb{E}[S_i S_{i+k}^\top]\) and estimating by sample quantities gives \[V := \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}\!\left(\bar{S}\right) = \frac{1}{n^2}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n S_i S_i^\top + \sum_{i=1}^{n}\!\left(S_i S_{i+1}^\top + S_{i+1} S_i^\top\right) + \sum_{i=1}^{n}\!\left(S_i S_{i+2}^\top + S_{i+2} S_i^\top\right)\right).\]
Parametric Bootstrap Test. Under \(H_0\), \(\bar{S} \approx N(0, V)\) by the CLT. This gives a direct procedure:
Consistency of \(V\). The parametric bootstrap is valid only if \(V\) consistently estimates \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar{S})\). If \(V\) is systematically too small, the bootstrap null distribution will be too narrow, producing an excess of small p-values. We check this by simulating many datasets under \(H_0\), computing the empirical variance of \(\bar{S}\) across replications, and comparing it to the average of the estimated \(V\). The two should agree.

title: 8  Parametric Bootstrap Test
text:
Compute the observed statistic \(T_\text{obs} = \max_{1 \leq j \leq p} |\bar{S}_j|\).
Draw \(S^{(b)} \sim N(0, V)\) for \(b = 1, \ldots, B\).
Compute \(T^{(b)} = \max_{1 \leq j \leq p} |S^{(b)}_j|\).
The p-value is \(\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^B \mathbf{1}\!\left[T^{(b)} \geq T_\text{obs}\right]\).

title: 9  Independence Test
text:
9.1 Classical Theory
The Pearson correlation test and its robust extensions follow a three-tier hierarchy based on what is assumed about the joint distribution.
Under Gaussianity, \(\rho = 0\) and \(X \perp Y\) are equivalent, so \(T = \sqrt{n-2}\,\hat\rho/\sqrt{1-\hat\rho^2}\) is an exact independence test. Without Gaussianity but under independence, \(\kappa_{22} = 1\) still holds at \(H_0: X \perp Y\), so \(\sqrt{n}\,\hat\rho \xrightarrow{d} N(0, 1)\). For the strictly weaker \(H_0: \rho = 0\) without assuming independence, \(\kappa_{22}\) must be estimated, giving asymptotic variance \[
v^2 = \frac{1}{n}\!\left(\omega_x^2 + \omega_y^2 + \kappa_{22} + \tfrac{5}{2}\right).
\]
The ECE test follows the same hierarchy: Gaussian or independent errors give \(\kappa_{22} = 1\); otherwise \(\hat\kappa_{22}\) is estimated via the MoM construction below.

title: 9  Independence Test
text:
9.2 Estimators for \(\kappa_{22}\)
Three estimators are developed below.






Regression



With \(T_k^{(2)}(X,Y) = \sum_i (X_i - X_{i+k})^2(Y_i - Y_{i+k})^2\), \[\begin{align}
\hat\kappa_{22}^{\mathrm{reg}} &= \frac{2T_1^{(2)}(X,Y) - T_2^{(2)}(X,Y)}{2n\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_y^2} - \frac{2\hat\sigma_{xy}^2}{\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_y^2} - 1 && \text{(general)} \\[4pt]
&= \frac{2T_1^{(2)}(X,Y) - T_2^{(2)}(X,Y)}{2n\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_y^2} - 1 && (H_0)
\end{align}\]








Matrix (\(\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\sigma_{xy})\))



\[\begin{align}
\hat\kappa_{22}^{V} &= \frac{n\,\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\sigma_{xy})}{\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_y^2} - \frac{3\hat\sigma_{xy}^2 + 4\hat\sigma_{xy}\hat\omega_{xy}}{2\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_y^2} - \frac{\hat\omega_x^2}{\hat\sigma_x^2} - \frac{\hat\omega_y^2}{\hat\sigma_y^2} - \frac{5}{2} && \text{(general)} \\[4pt]
&= \frac{n\,\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\hat\sigma_{xy})}{\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_y^2} - \frac{\hat\omega_x^2}{\hat\sigma_x^2} - \frac{\hat\omega_y^2}{\hat\sigma_y^2} - \frac{5}{2} && (H_0)
\end{align}\]








Method of Moments



\[\begin{align}
\hat\kappa_{22}^{\mathrm{MoM}} &= \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_i S_{xx,i}\,S_{yy,i}}{\bar S_{xx}\,\bar S_{yy}} - \frac{3\hat\sigma_{xy}^2 + 4\hat\sigma_{xy}\hat\omega_{xy}}{\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_y^2} && \text{(general)} \\[4pt]
&= \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_i S_{xx,i}\,S_{yy,i}}{\bar S_{xx}\,\bar S_{yy}} && (H_0)
\end{align}\]

title: 9  Independence Test
text:
9.3 Estimating \(\kappa_{22}\) via \(V\)

9.3.1 Estimating \(\kappa_{22}\) via \(V_{xy}\)
Let \(s_i^{(k)} = (X_i - X_{i+k})(Y_i - Y_{i+k})\) and \(S_i = \frac{s_i^{(1)} + s_{i+1}^{(1)} - s_i^{(2)}}{2}\) as in the Multiplier Bootstrap chapter, so that \[
\boxed{\bar{S} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n S_i = \frac{2T_1(X,Y) - T_2(X,Y)}{2n} = \hat\sigma_{xy}.}
\] Since \(S_i\) depends only on indices \(i-2, i-1, i\), terms at lags \(\ge 3\) are independent, so \[
\operatorname{Var}(\bar{S}) = \frac{1}{n^2}\!\left[\sum_i \operatorname{Var}(S_i) + 2\sum_i \operatorname{Cov}(S_i, S_{i+1}) + 2\sum_i \operatorname{Cov}(S_i, S_{i+2})\right].
\] Replacing each population quantity with its sample analog gives the lag-2 variance estimate \[
V := \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\bar{S}) = \frac{1}{n^2}\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n S_i^2 + \sum_{i=1}^n (S_i S_{i+1} + S_{i+1} S_i) + \sum_{i=1}^n (S_i S_{i+2} + S_{i+2} S_i)\right),
\] or in matrix form, writing \(\mathbf{S} = (S_1, \ldots, S_n)^\top\), \[
\boxed{V = \frac{1}{n^2}\,\mathbf{S}^\top(I + C_1 + C_1^\top + C_2 + C_2^\top)\mathbf{S}.}
\]
Since \(\bar S = (2T_1 - T_2)/(2n)\), we have \(V \approx \operatorname{Var}(2T_1 - T_2)/(4n^2)\). The variance on the right has a general closed form; under \(H_0\) (\(\sigma_{xy} = 0\)) it simplifies so we can solve for \(\kappa_{22}\) from \(V\).






Derivation: \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar{S})\) from \(\Sigma_Z\)





Since \(\bar{S} = (2T_1 - T_2)/(2n)\), \[
\operatorname{Var}(\bar{S}) = \frac{1}{4n^2}\bigl(4[\Sigma_Z]_{55} - 4[\Sigma_Z]_{56} + [\Sigma_Z]_{66}\bigr).
\] The general \(\Sigma_Z\) entries from the Z-Test chapter are \[[\Sigma_Z]_{55} = 2n\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2(2\kappa_{22}+1) - 2n\sigma_{xy}^2 + 2n\sigma_y^2\omega_x^2 + 2n\sigma_x^2\omega_y^2 + 4n\sigma_{xy}\omega_{xy},\] \[[\Sigma_Z]_{56} = 4n(\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2\kappa_{22} - \sigma_{xy}^2) + 2n\sigma_y^2\omega_x^2 + 2n\sigma_x^2\omega_y^2 + 4n\sigma_{xy}\omega_{xy},\] \[[\Sigma_Z]_{66} = 2n\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2(2\kappa_{22}+1) - 2n\sigma_{xy}^2 + 4n\sigma_y^2\omega_x^2 + 4n\sigma_x^2\omega_y^2 + 8n\sigma_{xy}\omega_{xy}.\] Substituting and collecting terms gives the general expression \[\operatorname{Var}(\bar{S}) = \frac{1}{2n}\bigl[(2\kappa_{22}+5)\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 3\sigma_{xy}^2 + 4\sigma_{xy}\omega_{xy} + 2\sigma_y^2\omega_x^2 + 2\sigma_x^2\omega_y^2\bigr].\] Under \(H_0\) (\(\sigma_{xy} = 0\)) the last two terms vanish, yielding \[\operatorname{Var}(\bar{S}) = \frac{1}{2n}\bigl[(2\kappa_{22}+5)\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 2\sigma_y^2\omega_x^2 + 2\sigma_x^2\omega_y^2\bigr]. \qquad\square\]



Since \(V \approx \operatorname{Var}(\bar{S})\), substituting the general expression and solving gives \[\boxed{\hat\kappa_{22} = \frac{nV}{\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_y^2} - \frac{3}{2}\frac{\hat\sigma_{xy}^2}{\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_y^2} - \frac{2\hat\sigma_{xy}\hat\omega_{xy}}{\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_y^2} - \frac{\hat\omega_x^2}{\hat\sigma_x^2} - \frac{\hat\omega_y^2}{\hat\sigma_y^2} - \frac{5}{2}.}\] Under \(H_0\) (\(\hat\sigma_{xy} = 0\)) the middle two terms vanish, yielding \[\hat\kappa_{22} = \frac{nV}{\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_y^2} - \frac{\hat\omega_x^2}{\hat\sigma_x^2} - \frac{\hat\omega_y^2}{\hat\sigma_y^2} - \frac{5}{2}.\]






Simulation: Verifying \(\hat\kappa_{22}\) via \(V_{xy}\)






Independent (\(\kappa_{22} = 1\))Dependent (\(\kappa_{22} = 5\))\(\lambda\)-Mixing


Scenario 2, \(L = 4\), Gaussian independent errors. Under independence \(\kappa_{22} = 1\) regardless of marginals.











Using \(\varepsilon_y = (\varepsilon_x^2 - 1)/\sqrt{2}\) with \(\varepsilon_x \sim N(0,1)\), giving \(\sigma_{xy} = 0\) and \(\kappa_{22} = 5\).











Using \(\varepsilon_y = \lambda(\varepsilon_x^2-1)/\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{1-\lambda^2}\,\eta\) with \(\varepsilon_x, \eta \stackrel{iid}{\sim} N(0,1)\), which gives \(\sigma_{xy} = 0\) and \(\kappa_{22} = 1 + 4\lambda^2\).

















9.3.2 Estimating \(\kappa_{22}\) via \(V_{12}\)
An alternative estimator uses the cross-covariance \(V_{12} = \widehat{\mathrm{Cov}}(\bar S^{xx}, \bar S^{yy})\) in place of \(V_{xy}\). Since \(S_{xx} = (2T_1(X,X) - T_2(X,X))/(2n)\) and \(S_{yy} = (2T_1(Y,Y) - T_2(Y,Y))/(2n)\),
\[
\mathrm{Cov}(S_{xx}, S_{yy}) = \frac{1}{4n^2}\,\mathrm{Cov}\!\bigl(2T_1(X,X) - T_2(X,X),\; 2T_1(Y,Y) - T_2(Y,Y)\bigr).
\]
Expanding by bilinearity gives a linear combination of the four cross-diagonal \(\Sigma_Z\) entries:
\[
4\,[\Sigma_Z]_{T_1(X,X),T_1(Y,Y)} - 2\,[\Sigma_Z]_{T_1(X,X),T_2(Y,Y)} - 2\,[\Sigma_Z]_{T_2(X,X),T_1(Y,Y)} + [\Sigma_Z]_{T_2(X,X),T_2(Y,Y)}.
\]
All four entries share the coefficient \(4n\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2\) on \((\kappa_{22}-1)\); the \(\omega_{xy}\) terms cancel to \(16n\sigma_{xy}\omega_{xy}\) and the \(\sigma_{xy}^2\) terms collect to \(8n\sigma_{xy}^2\). Dividing through by \(4n^2\) gives the closed form
\[
\mathrm{Cov}(S_{xx}, S_{yy}) = \frac{1}{n}\!\left[\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2(\kappa_{22}-1) + 2\sigma_{xy}^2 + 4\sigma_{xy}\omega_{xy}\right].
\]
Solving for \(\kappa_{22}\),
\[
\boxed{\hat\kappa_{22} = \frac{nV_{12} - 2\hat\sigma_{xy}^2 - 4\hat\sigma_{xy}\hat\omega_{xy}}{\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_y^2} + 1,}
\]
which under \(H_0: \rho = 0\) reduces to \(\hat\kappa_{22} = nV_{12}/(\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_y^2) + 1\), free of all \(\omega\) corrections.


9.3.3 Estimating \(\kappa_{40}\) via \(V_{xx}\)
Applying the same construction to \((X, X)\) in place of \((X, Y)\): let \(s_i^{(k)} = (X_i - X_{i+k})^2\) and \(S_i^{xx} = (s_i^{(1)} + s_{i+1}^{(1)} - s_i^{(2)})/2\), so that \(\bar S^{xx} = (2T_1(X,X) - T_2(X,X))/(2n) = \hat\sigma_x^2\). Define \[
V_{xx} := \widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\bar S^{xx}) = \frac{1}{n^2}\,(\tilde{\mathbf{S}}^{xx})^\top(I + C_1 + C_1^\top + C_2 + C_2^\top)\tilde{\mathbf{S}}^{xx}, \qquad \tilde S_i^{xx} = S_i^{xx} - \bar S^{xx}.
\]






Derivation: \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar{S}^{xx})\) from \(\Sigma_Z\)





Since \(\bar{S}^{xx} = (2T_1(X,X) - T_2(X,X))/(2n)\), \[
\operatorname{Var}(\bar{S}^{xx}) = \frac{1}{4n^2}\bigl(4[\Sigma_Z]_{11} - 4[\Sigma_Z]_{12} + [\Sigma_Z]_{22}\bigr).
\] Substituting the entries from the Z-Test chapter: \[[\Sigma_Z]_{11} = 4n\kappa_{40}\sigma_x^4 + 8n\sigma_x^2\omega_x^2,\] \[[\Sigma_Z]_{12} = 4n(\kappa_{40}-1)\sigma_x^4 + 8n\sigma_x^2\omega_x^2,\] \[[\Sigma_Z]_{22} = 4n\kappa_{40}\sigma_x^4 + 16n\sigma_x^2\omega_x^2.\] Collecting terms: \[\operatorname{Var}(\bar{S}^{xx}) = \frac{1}{n}\bigl[(\kappa_{40}+4)\sigma_x^4 + 4\sigma_x^2\omega_x^2\bigr]. \qquad\square\]



Since \(V_{xx} \approx \operatorname{Var}(\bar{S}^{xx})\), substituting and solving gives \[
\boxed{\hat\kappa_{40} = \frac{nV_{xx}}{\hat\sigma_x^4} - \frac{4\hat\omega_x^2}{\hat\sigma_x^2} - 4.}
\] By symmetry (\(x \leftrightarrow y\)), the same construction applied to \((Y, Y)\) yields \(\hat\kappa_{04} = nV_{yy}/\hat\sigma_y^4 - 4\hat\omega_y^2/\hat\sigma_y^2 - 4\).






Simulation: Verifying \(\hat\kappa_{40}\)






Gaussian (\(\kappa_{40} = 3\))Exponential (\(\kappa_{40} = 9\))\(\lambda\)-Mixing


Scenario 2, \(L = 4\), Gaussian errors (\(\kappa_{40} = 3\)).











Scenario 2, \(L = 4\), exponential errors (\(\kappa_{40} = 9\)).











Using \(\varepsilon_x = \lambda(z^2-1)/\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{1-\lambda^2}\,w\) with \(z, w \stackrel{iid}{\sim} N(0,1)\), which gives \(\kappa_{40} = 12\lambda^4 + 3\).

















9.3.4 Estimating \(\kappa_{31}\) via \(C_{xx,xy}\)
The cumulant \(\kappa_{31}\) appears in the cross-covariances between the \((X,X)\) and \((X,Y)\) blocks of \(\Sigma_Z\). Define the lag-2 cross-covariance \[
C_{xx,xy} := \frac{1}{n^2}\,(\tilde{\mathbf{S}}^{xx})^\top(I + C_1 + C_1^\top + C_2 + C_2^\top)\tilde{\mathbf{S}}^{xy}, \qquad \tilde S_i^{xx} = S_i^{xx} - \bar S^{xx},\quad \tilde S_i^{xy} = S_i^{xy} - \bar S^{xy},
\] which estimates \(\operatorname{Cov}(\bar S^{xx}, \bar S^{xy})\).






Derivation: \(\operatorname{Cov}(\bar{S}^{xx}, \bar{S}^{xy})\) from \(\Sigma_Z\)





Since \(\bar{S}^{xx} = (2T_1(X,X) - T_2(X,X))/(2n)\) and \(\bar{S}^{xy} = (2T_1(X,Y) - T_2(X,Y))/(2n)\), \[
\operatorname{Cov}(\bar{S}^{xx}, \bar{S}^{xy}) = \frac{1}{4n^2}\bigl(4[\Sigma_Z]_{15} - 2[\Sigma_Z]_{16} - 2[\Sigma_Z]_{25} + [\Sigma_Z]_{26}\bigr).
\] The relevant entries from the Z-Test chapter are \[[\Sigma_Z]_{15} = 4n\sigma_x^3\sigma_y\kappa_{31} + 4n\sigma_{xy}\omega_x^2 + 4n\sigma_x^2\omega_{xy},\] \[[\Sigma_Z]_{16} = 4n\sigma_x^3\sigma_y\kappa_{31} - 4n\sigma_x^2\sigma_{xy} + 4n\sigma_{xy}\omega_x^2 + 4n\sigma_x^2\omega_{xy},\] \[[\Sigma_Z]_{25} = 4n\sigma_x^3\sigma_y\kappa_{31} - 4n\sigma_x^2\sigma_{xy} + 4n\sigma_{xy}\omega_x^2 + 4n\sigma_x^2\omega_{xy},\] \[[\Sigma_Z]_{26} = 4n\sigma_x^3\sigma_y\kappa_{31} + 8n\sigma_{xy}\omega_x^2 + 8n\sigma_x^2\omega_{xy}.\] Collecting terms: \[\operatorname{Cov}(\bar{S}^{xx}, \bar{S}^{xy}) = \frac{1}{n}\bigl[\sigma_x^3\sigma_y\kappa_{31} + 4\sigma_x^2\sigma_{xy} + 2\sigma_{xy}\omega_x^2 + 2\sigma_x^2\omega_{xy}\bigr]. \qquad\square\]



Since \(C_{xx,xy} \approx \operatorname{Cov}(\bar{S}^{xx}, \bar{S}^{xy})\), substituting and solving gives \[
\hat\kappa_{31} = \frac{nC_{xx,xy}}{\hat\sigma_x^3\hat\sigma_y} - \frac{4\hat\sigma_{xy}}{\hat\sigma_x\hat\sigma_y} - \frac{2\hat\sigma_{xy}\hat\omega_x^2}{\hat\sigma_x^3\hat\sigma_y} - \frac{2\hat\omega_{xy}}{\hat\sigma_x\hat\sigma_y}.
\] By symmetry (\(x \leftrightarrow y\)), the same construction with \(C_{yy,xy}\) yields \(\hat\kappa_{13}\).






Simulation: Verifying \(\hat\kappa_{31}\)






Independent (\(\kappa_{31} = 0\))Dependent (\(\kappa_{31} = 3\))\(\lambda\)-Mixing


Scenario 2, \(L = 4\), Gaussian independent errors. Under independence \(\kappa_{31} = 0\).











Using \(\varepsilon_y = \varepsilon_x\) with \(\varepsilon_x \sim N(0,1)\), giving \(\sigma_{xy} = \sigma_x^2\) and \(\kappa_{31} = \kappa_{40} = 3\).











Using \(\varepsilon_y = \lambda\varepsilon_x + \sqrt{1-\lambda^2}\,\eta\) with \(\varepsilon_x, \eta \stackrel{iid}{\sim} N(0,1)\), which gives \(\kappa_{31} = 3\lambda\).

title: 9  Independence Test
text:
9.4 Estimating \(\kappa_{22}\) via Moments
Under the ECE model \(X_i = \theta_{x,i} + \varepsilon_{x,i}\), \(Y_i = \theta_{y,i} + \varepsilon_{y,i}\) with iid mean-zero errors, define \(\kappa_{22} = E[\varepsilon_{x,i}^2\varepsilon_{y,i}^2]/(\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2)\), which equals 1 under independence. Write \(T_k(\theta_x, \theta_y) = \sum_{i=1}^n (\theta_{x,i} - \theta_{x,i+k})(\theta_{y,i} - \theta_{y,i+k})\) for the signal-difference inner product and \[
\boxed{T_k^{(2)}(X, Y) = \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - X_{i+k})^2(Y_i - Y_{i+k})^2}
\] for its squared analog (applicable to any pair of sequences).
The strategy is to compute \(E[T_k^{(2)}(X, Y)]\) exactly and solve for \(\kappa_{22}\).






Lemma: \(\operatorname{Cov}\bigl((X_i - X_{i+k})^2,\,(Y_i - Y_{i+k})^2\bigr)\)





Write \(X_i - X_{i+k} = (\theta_{x,i} - \theta_{x,i+k}) + (\varepsilon_{x,i} - \varepsilon_{x,i+k})\) and \(Y_i - Y_{i+k} = (\theta_{y,i} - \theta_{y,i+k}) + (\varepsilon_{y,i} - \varepsilon_{y,i+k})\). Since the signal differences are constants, \[
\begin{aligned}
&\operatorname{Cov}\bigl((X_i-X_{i+k})^2,\,(Y_i-Y_{i+k})^2\bigr) \\
&\quad= 4(\theta_{x,i}-\theta_{x,i+k})(\theta_{y,i}-\theta_{y,i+k})\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_{x,i}-\varepsilon_{x,i+k},\,\varepsilon_{y,i}-\varepsilon_{y,i+k}) \\
&\quad\phantom{=}\; + 2(\theta_{x,i}-\theta_{x,i+k})\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_{x,i}-\varepsilon_{x,i+k},\,(\varepsilon_{y,i}-\varepsilon_{y,i+k})^2) \\
&\quad\phantom{=}\; + 2(\theta_{y,i}-\theta_{y,i+k})\operatorname{Cov}((\varepsilon_{x,i}-\varepsilon_{x,i+k})^2,\,\varepsilon_{y,i}-\varepsilon_{y,i+k}) \\
&\quad\phantom{=}\; + \operatorname{Cov}((\varepsilon_{x,i}-\varepsilon_{x,i+k})^2,\,(\varepsilon_{y,i}-\varepsilon_{y,i+k})^2).
\end{aligned}
\] The four pieces:

\(\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_{x,i}-\varepsilon_{x,i+k},\,\varepsilon_{y,i}-\varepsilon_{y,i+k}) = \sigma_{xy} + \sigma_{xy} = 2\sigma_{xy}\).
\(\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_{x,i}-\varepsilon_{x,i+k},\,(\varepsilon_{y,i}-\varepsilon_{y,i+k})^2) = 0\): since \(E[\varepsilon_{x,i}-\varepsilon_{x,i+k}] = 0\), this equals \(E[(\varepsilon_{x,i}-\varepsilon_{x,i+k})(\varepsilon_{y,i}-\varepsilon_{y,i+k})^2]\). Swapping \(i \leftrightarrow i+k\) negates \(\varepsilon_{x,i}-\varepsilon_{x,i+k}\) but fixes \((\varepsilon_{y,i}-\varepsilon_{y,i+k})^2\); since the pairs are iid the expectation is unchanged, so it equals its own negative and must be 0. By symmetry \(\operatorname{Cov}((\varepsilon_{x,i}-\varepsilon_{x,i+k})^2,\,\varepsilon_{y,i}-\varepsilon_{y,i+k}) = 0\).
For \(\operatorname{Cov}((\varepsilon_{x,i}-\varepsilon_{x,i+k})^2,\,(\varepsilon_{y,i}-\varepsilon_{y,i+k})^2)\): expanding using independence between time \(i\) and time \(i+k\) (and mean-zero errors), \[
E[(\varepsilon_{x,i}-\varepsilon_{x,i+k})^2(\varepsilon_{y,i}-\varepsilon_{y,i+k})^2] = 2E[\varepsilon_{x}^2\varepsilon_{y}^2] + 2\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 4\sigma_{xy}^2 = 2\kappa_{22}\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 2\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 4\sigma_{xy}^2,
\] while \(E[(\varepsilon_{x,i}-\varepsilon_{x,i+k})^2]E[(\varepsilon_{y,i}-\varepsilon_{y,i+k})^2] = 4\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2\), so \(\operatorname{Cov}((\varepsilon_{x,i}-\varepsilon_{x,i+k})^2,\,(\varepsilon_{y,i}-\varepsilon_{y,i+k})^2) = 2(\kappa_{22}-1)\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 4\sigma_{xy}^2\).

Combining: \[
\operatorname{Cov}\bigl((X_i-X_{i+k})^2,\,(Y_i-Y_{i+k})^2\bigr) = 8\sigma_{xy}(\theta_{x,i}-\theta_{x,i+k})(\theta_{y,i}-\theta_{y,i+k}) + 2(\kappa_{22}-1)\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 4\sigma_{xy}^2. \qquad\square
\]









Lemma: \(E[T_k^{(2)}(X, Y)]\)





Exact expectation. Applying \(E[AB] = \operatorname{Cov}(A,B) + E[A]E[B]\) to each term and summing, using the lemma and \(E\!\left[\sum_i(X_i-X_{i+k})^2\right] = T_k(\theta_x,\theta_x) + 2n\sigma_x^2\): \[
\begin{aligned}
E[T_k^{(2)}(X, Y)]
&= 2n(\kappa_{22}-1)\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 8\sigma_{xy}T_k(\theta_x,\theta_y) + 4n\sigma_{xy}^2 \\
&\quad + T_k^{(2)}(\theta_x, \theta_y) + 2\sigma_y^2 T_k(\theta_x,\theta_x) + 2\sigma_x^2 T_k(\theta_y,\theta_y) + 4n\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2.
\end{aligned}
\]






Simulation: Verifying \(E[T_k^{(2)}(X, Y)]\)





We simulate 1000 datasets from scenario 2 with \(n = 500\) observations, \(L = 4\) change points (frequent relative to \(n\)), exponential errors, and heterogeneous marginal variances (\(\sigma_x^2 = 4\), \(\sigma_y^2 = 0.25\)). For each dataset we compute \(T_2^{(2)}(X, Y)\) and compare its distribution to the formula value (red line).





















Remark



As with \(2T_1(\theta_x,\theta_y) - T_2(\theta_x,\theta_y) = 0\), we have \(2T_1^{(2)}(\theta_x,\theta_y) - T_2^{(2)}(\theta_x,\theta_y) = 0\).


Linear combination. Applying the exact expectation at \(k=1\) and \(k=2\) and forming \(2E[T_1^{(2)}(X,Y)] - E[T_2^{(2)}(X,Y)]\), all \(\theta\)-dependent terms vanish by the remark and the standard property applied to \((X,X)\) and \((Y,Y)\): \[
2E[T_1^{(2)}(X,Y)] - E[T_2^{(2)}(X,Y)] =
\boxed{2n(\kappa_{22}+1)\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 4n\sigma_{xy}^2.}
\]
Solving for \(\kappa_{22}\): \[
\kappa_{22} = \frac{2E[T_1^{(2)}(X,Y)] - E[T_2^{(2)}(X,Y)]}{2n\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2} - \frac{2\sigma_{xy}^2}{\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2} - 1.
\]
Plugging in estimates: \[
\boxed{
\hat\kappa_{22} = \frac{2T_1^{(2)}(X,Y) - T_2^{(2)}(X,Y)}{2n\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_y^2} - \frac{2\hat\sigma_{xy}^2}{\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_y^2} - 1.
}
\]






Simulation: Verifying \(\hat\kappa_{22}\) (Lag Product)





We simulate 10,000 datasets from scenario 2 with \(L = 4\) change points, exponential errors, and heterogeneous marginal variances (\(\sigma_x^2 = 4\), \(\sigma_y^2 = 0.25\)). The sample mean of \(\hat\kappa_{22}\) (dashed) should fall on the true value (red).

title: 9  Independence Test
text:
9.5 Method of Moments via \(S_i\) Terms
The method-of-moments estimator for \(\kappa_{22} = E[\varepsilon_x^2\varepsilon_y^2]/(\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2)\) plugs in squared residuals directly: \[\hat\kappa_{22} = \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_i \varepsilon_{x,i}^2\,\varepsilon_{y,i}^2}{\hat\sigma_x^2\,\hat\sigma_y^2}.\] When there are no change points, \(\varepsilon_{x,i}\) and \(\varepsilon_{y,i}\) are observable as demeaned residuals, and this estimator is consistent.
Under change points, the mean \(\theta_{x,i}\) varies over time, so \(X_i - \bar X\) is contaminated by jumps and \(\varepsilon_{x,i}\) is not directly observable. We need surrogates for \(\varepsilon_{x,i}^2\) and \(\varepsilon_{y,i}^2\) that have constant expectation \(\sigma_x^2\) and \(\sigma_y^2\) at every index regardless of change-point amplitudes.
Recall from the multiplier bootstrap that \[S_i = \frac{s_i^{(1)} + s_{i+1}^{(1)} - s_i^{(2)}}{2}, \qquad s_i^{(k)} = (X_i - X_{i+k})(Y_i - Y_{i+k}),\] satisfies \(E[S_i] = \sigma_{xy}\) regardless of change-point amplitudes. Applying the same construction to each series separately gives \[S_{xx,i} = \frac{(X_i-X_{i+1})^2 + (X_{i+1}-X_{i+2})^2 - (X_i-X_{i+2})^2}{2}, \qquad S_{yy,i} = \frac{(Y_i-Y_{i+1})^2 + (Y_{i+1}-Y_{i+2})^2 - (Y_i-Y_{i+2})^2}{2},\] with \(E[S_{xx,i}] = \sigma_x^2\) and \(E[S_{yy,i}] = \sigma_y^2\) at every index, change points included. Substituting these as surrogates for \(\varepsilon_{x,i}^2\) and \(\varepsilon_{y,i}^2\) gives the ECE MoM estimator: \[\hat\kappa_{22}^{\mathrm{MoM}} = \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_i S_{xx,i}\,S_{yy,i}}{\bar S_{xx}\,\bar S_{yy}}.\]
The \(S_i\) terms are autocorrelated at lags 1 and 2 (consecutive terms share observations), so \(\frac{1}{n}\sum S_{xx,i}S_{yy,i}\) has inflated variance relative to an i.i.d. average. The estimator is consistent for \(\kappa_{22}\) under the null \(\sigma_{xy}=0\) — the regime relevant to the independence test (proof below). For \(\sigma_{xy}\neq 0\) the surrogate product carries an \(O(\rho^2)\) bias, so \(\hat\kappa_{22}^{\mathrm{MoM}}\) targets \(\kappa_{22}+3\rho^2+\rho\,\bar B/(\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2)\) rather than \(\kappa_{22}\).






Consistency under \(\sigma_{xy}=0\): \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_i S_{xx,i}S_{yy,i} \xrightarrow{p} E[\varepsilon_x^2\varepsilon_y^2]\)





Definitions. Write \(X_i - X_{i+k} = h_{x,i}^{(k)} + e_{x,i}^{(k)}\), where \(h_{x,i}^{(k)} = \theta_{x,i} - \theta_{x,i+k}\) is the signal difference and \(e_{x,i}^{(k)} = \varepsilon_{x,i} - \varepsilon_{x,i+k}\) is the noise difference. Define the squared differences \[s_{x,i}^{(k)} = \bigl(X_i - X_{i+k}\bigr)^2 = \bigl(h_{x,i}^{(k)} + e_{x,i}^{(k)}\bigr)^2,\] and likewise \(s_{y,i}^{(k)} = (Y_i - Y_{i+k})^2 = (h_{y,i}^{(k)} + e_{y,i}^{(k)})^2\). Then \[S_{xx,i} = \frac{s_{x,i}^{(1)} + s_{x,i+1}^{(1)} - s_{x,i}^{(2)}}{2}, \qquad S_{yy,i} = \frac{s_{y,i}^{(1)} + s_{y,i+1}^{(1)} - s_{y,i}^{(2)}}{2}.\]
Expanding the product. Multiplying out gives \[4\,S_{xx,i}\,S_{yy,i} = s_{x,i}^{(1)}s_{y,i}^{(1)} + s_{x,i}^{(1)}s_{y,i+1}^{(1)} - s_{x,i}^{(1)}s_{y,i}^{(2)} + s_{x,i+1}^{(1)}s_{y,i}^{(1)} + s_{x,i+1}^{(1)}s_{y,i+1}^{(1)} - s_{x,i+1}^{(1)}s_{y,i}^{(2)} - s_{x,i}^{(2)}s_{y,i}^{(1)} - s_{x,i}^{(2)}s_{y,i+1}^{(1)} + s_{x,i}^{(2)}s_{y,i}^{(2)}.\]
General term. It suffices to analyze \(E[s_{x,i}^{(k)}\,s_{y,j}^{(r)}]\) for general starting indices \(i,j\) and lags \(k,r\). Substituting the signal–noise decomposition and expanding each square gives nine terms: \[
s_{x,i}^{(k)}\,s_{y,j}^{(r)} = \begin{array}{lll}
(h_{x,i}^{(k)})^2(h_{y,j}^{(r)})^2 & +\; 2(h_{x,i}^{(k)})^2 h_{y,j}^{(r)} e_{y,j}^{(r)} & +\; (h_{x,i}^{(k)})^2(e_{y,j}^{(r)})^2 \\[6pt]
+\; 2h_{x,i}^{(k)} e_{x,i}^{(k)} (h_{y,j}^{(r)})^2 & +\; 4h_{x,i}^{(k)} h_{y,j}^{(r)} e_{x,i}^{(k)} e_{y,j}^{(r)} & +\; 2h_{x,i}^{(k)} e_{x,i}^{(k)}(e_{y,j}^{(r)})^2 \\[6pt]
+\; (e_{x,i}^{(k)})^2(h_{y,j}^{(r)})^2 & +\; 2(e_{x,i}^{(k)})^2 h_{y,j}^{(r)} e_{y,j}^{(r)} & +\; (e_{x,i}^{(k)})^2(e_{y,j}^{(r)})^2.
\end{array}
\] Taking expectations and using \(E[e_{x,i}^{(k)}] = E[e_{y,j}^{(r)}] = 0\) to drop the terms in position (1,2) and (2,1) of the grid, seven terms remain: \[\begin{align}
E[s_{x,i}^{(k)}\,s_{y,j}^{(r)}]
&= (h_{x,i}^{(k)})^2(h_{y,j}^{(r)})^2 \\
&\quad+ (h_{x,i}^{(k)})^2\,E[(e_{y,j}^{(r)})^2] + (h_{y,j}^{(r)})^2\,E[(e_{x,i}^{(k)})^2] \\
&\quad+ 4h_{x,i}^{(k)}h_{y,j}^{(r)}\,E[e_{x,i}^{(k)}\,e_{y,j}^{(r)}] \\
&\quad+ 2h_{x,i}^{(k)}\,E[e_{x,i}^{(k)}(e_{y,j}^{(r)})^2] + 2h_{y,j}^{(r)}\,E[(e_{x,i}^{(k)})^2 e_{y,j}^{(r)}] \\
&\quad+ E[(e_{x,i}^{(k)})^2(e_{y,j}^{(r)})^2].
\end{align}\]
Case 1: \(i = j\), \(k = r\). Both increments span the same pair of time indices, so \(e_{x,i}^{(k)}\) and \(e_{y,i}^{(k)}\) involve \((\varepsilon_{x,i}, \varepsilon_{y,i})\) and \((\varepsilon_{x,i+k}, \varepsilon_{y,i+k})\). By iid: \[\begin{align}
E[(e_{x,i}^{(k)})^2] &= 2\sigma_x^2, \qquad E[(e_{y,i}^{(k)})^2] = 2\sigma_y^2, \\
E[e_{x,i}^{(k)}\,e_{y,i}^{(k)}] &= 2\sigma_{xy}, \\
E[e_{x,i}^{(k)}(e_{y,i}^{(k)})^2] &= 0, \qquad E[(e_{x,i}^{(k)})^2\,e_{y,i}^{(k)}] = 0, \\
E[(e_{x,i}^{(k)})^2(e_{y,i}^{(k)})^2] &= 2\kappa_{22}\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 2\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 4\sigma_{xy}^2.
\end{align}\] Substituting into the general formula: \[E[s_{x,i}^{(k)}\,s_{y,i}^{(k)}] = (h_{x,i}^{(k)})^2(h_{y,i}^{(k)})^2 + 2\sigma_y^2(h_{x,i}^{(k)})^2 + 2\sigma_x^2(h_{y,i}^{(k)})^2 + 8\sigma_{xy}\,h_{x,i}^{(k)}\,h_{y,i}^{(k)} + 2\kappa_{22}\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 2\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 4\sigma_{xy}^2.\]
Case 2: \(j = i+1\), \(k = r = 1\). The increments \(e_{x,i}^{(1)} = \varepsilon_{x,i} - \varepsilon_{x,i+1}\) and \(e_{y,i+1}^{(1)} = \varepsilon_{y,i+1} - \varepsilon_{y,i+2}\) share only time index \(i+1\). By iid: \[\begin{align}
E[(e_{x,i}^{(1)})^2] &= 2\sigma_x^2, \qquad E[(e_{y,i+1}^{(1)})^2] = 2\sigma_y^2, \\
E[e_{x,i}^{(1)}\,e_{y,i+1}^{(1)}] &= -\sigma_{xy}, \\
E[e_{x,i}^{(1)}(e_{y,i+1}^{(1)})^2] &= -E[\varepsilon_x\varepsilon_y^2], \qquad E[(e_{x,i}^{(1)})^2\,e_{y,i+1}^{(1)}] = E[\varepsilon_x^2\varepsilon_y], \\
E[(e_{x,i}^{(1)})^2(e_{y,i+1}^{(1)})^2] &= \kappa_{22}\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 3\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2.
\end{align}\] Substituting into the general formula: \[\begin{align}
E[s_{x,i}^{(1)}\,s_{y,i+1}^{(1)}] &= (h_{x,i}^{(1)})^2(h_{y,i+1}^{(1)})^2 + 2\sigma_y^2(h_{x,i}^{(1)})^2 + 2\sigma_x^2(h_{y,i+1}^{(1)})^2 - 4\sigma_{xy}\,h_{x,i}^{(1)}\,h_{y,i+1}^{(1)} \\
&\quad - 2h_{x,i}^{(1)}\,E[\varepsilon_x\varepsilon_y^2] + 2h_{y,i+1}^{(1)}\,E[\varepsilon_x^2\varepsilon_y] + \kappa_{22}\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 3\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2.
\end{align}\]
Case 3: \(i = j\), \(k = 1\), \(r = 2\). The increments \(e_{x,i}^{(1)} = \varepsilon_{x,i} - \varepsilon_{x,i+1}\) and \(e_{y,i}^{(2)} = \varepsilon_{y,i} - \varepsilon_{y,i+2}\) share only time index \(i\). By iid: \[\begin{align}
E[(e_{x,i}^{(1)})^2] &= 2\sigma_x^2, \qquad E[(e_{y,i}^{(2)})^2] = 2\sigma_y^2, \\
E[e_{x,i}^{(1)}\,e_{y,i}^{(2)}] &= \sigma_{xy}, \\
E[e_{x,i}^{(1)}(e_{y,i}^{(2)})^2] &= E[\varepsilon_x\varepsilon_y^2], \qquad E[(e_{x,i}^{(1)})^2\,e_{y,i}^{(2)}] = E[\varepsilon_x^2\varepsilon_y], \\
E[(e_{x,i}^{(1)})^2(e_{y,i}^{(2)})^2] &= \kappa_{22}\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 3\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2.
\end{align}\] Substituting into the general formula: \[\begin{align}
E[s_{x,i}^{(1)}\,s_{y,i}^{(2)}] &= (h_{x,i}^{(1)})^2(h_{y,i}^{(2)})^2 + 2\sigma_y^2(h_{x,i}^{(1)})^2 + 2\sigma_x^2(h_{y,i}^{(2)})^2 + 4\sigma_{xy}\,h_{x,i}^{(1)}\,h_{y,i}^{(2)} \\
&\quad + 2h_{x,i}^{(1)}\,E[\varepsilon_x\varepsilon_y^2] + 2h_{y,i}^{(2)}\,E[\varepsilon_x^2\varepsilon_y] + \kappa_{22}\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 3\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2.

Case 4: \(j = i+1\) (i.e. \(j \neq i\)), \(k = 1\), \(r = 2\). The increments \(e_{x,i+1}^{(1)} = \varepsilon_{x,i+1} - \varepsilon_{x,i+2}\) and \(e_{y,i}^{(2)} = \varepsilon_{y,i} - \varepsilon_{y,i+2}\) share only time index \(i+2\), which appears with a \(-\) sign in both. By iid: \[\begin{align}
E[(e_{x,i+1}^{(1)})^2] &= 2\sigma_x^2, \qquad E[(e_{y,i}^{(2)})^2] = 2\sigma_y^2, \\
E[e_{x,i+1}^{(1)}\,e_{y,i}^{(2)}] &= \sigma_{xy}, \\
E[e_{x,i+1}^{(1)}(e_{y,i}^{(2)})^2] &= -E[\varepsilon_x\varepsilon_y^2], \qquad E[(e_{x,i+1}^{(1)})^2\,e_{y,i}^{(2)}] = -E[\varepsilon_x^2\varepsilon_y], \\
E[(e_{x,i+1}^{(1)})^2(e_{y,i}^{(2)})^2] &= \kappa_{22}\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 3\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2.
\end{align}\] Substituting into the general formula: \[\begin{align}
E[s_{x,i+1}^{(1)}\,s_{y,i}^{(2)}] &= (h_{x,i+1}^{(1)})^2(h_{y,i}^{(2)})^2 + 2\sigma_y^2(h_{x,i+1}^{(1)})^2 + 2\sigma_x^2(h_{y,i}^{(2)})^2 + 4\sigma_{xy}\,h_{x,i+1}^{(1)}\,h_{y,i}^{(2)} \\
&\quad - 2h_{x,i+1}^{(1)}\,E[\varepsilon_x\varepsilon_y^2] - 2h_{y,i}^{(2)}\,E[\varepsilon_x^2\varepsilon_y] + \kappa_{22}\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 3\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2.
\end{align}\]
Assembling the sum. Substituting each case result into \(4E[S_{xx,i}S_{yy,i}]\) and grouping by term type: \[\begin{align}

&= \bigl[(h_{x,i}^{(1)})^2 + (h_{x,i+1}^{(1)})^2 - (h_{x,i}^{(2)})^2\bigr]\bigl[(h_{y,i}^{(1)})^2 + (h_{y,i+1}^{(1)})^2 - (h_{y,i}^{(2)})^2\bigr] \\
&\quad + 2\sigma_y^2\bigl[(h_{x,i}^{(1)})^2 + (h_{x,i+1}^{(1)})^2 - (h_{x,i}^{(2)})^2\bigr] + 2\sigma_x^2\bigl[(h_{y,i}^{(1)})^2 + (h_{y,i+1}^{(1)})^2 - (h_{y,i}^{(2)})^2\bigr] \\
&\quad + \sigma_{xy}\bigl[8h_{x,i}^{(1)}h_{y,i}^{(1)} - 4h_{x,i}^{(1)}h_{y,i+1}^{(1)} - 4h_{x,i}^{(1)}h_{y,i}^{(2)} - 4h_{x,i+1}^{(1)}h_{y,i}^{(1)} + 8h_{x,i+1}^{(1)}h_{y,i+1}^{(1)} \\
&\qquad\qquad - 4h_{x,i+1}^{(1)}h_{y,i}^{(2)} - 4h_{x,i}^{(2)}h_{y,i}^{(1)} - 4h_{x,i}^{(2)}h_{y,i+1}^{(1)} + 8h_{x,i}^{(2)}h_{y,i}^{(2)}\bigr] \\

&\quad + 3(2\kappa_{22}\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 2\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 4\sigma_{xy}^2) - 2(\kappa_{22}\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 3\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2).
\end{align}\]
Simplification. The first two lines each contain the factor \((h_{x,i}^{(1)})^2 + (h_{x,i+1}^{(1)})^2 - (h_{x,i}^{(2)})^2\). We claim \[\boxed{(h_{x,i}^{(1)})^2 + (h_{x,i+1}^{(1)})^2 - (h_{x,i}^{(2)})^2 = 0.}\] From the linear identity \(h_{x,i}^{(1)} + h_{x,i+1}^{(1)} - h_{x,i}^{(2)} = 0\) we have \(h_{x,i}^{(2)} = h_{x,i}^{(1)} + h_{x,i+1}^{(1)}\), so \[(h_{x,i}^{(1)})^2 + (h_{x,i+1}^{(1)})^2 - (h_{x,i}^{(2)})^2 = (h_{x,i}^{(1)})^2 + (h_{x,i+1}^{(1)})^2 - (h_{x,i}^{(1)} + h_{x,i+1}^{(1)})^2 = -2h_{x,i}^{(1)}h_{x,i+1}^{(1)}.\] This is not yet zero, but under the minimum segment length 2 assumption consecutive lag-1 differences cannot both be nonzero, so \(h_{x,i}^{(1)}h_{x,i+1}^{(1)} = 0\) at every index. The same argument applies to \(y\), so the first two lines both vanish. Collecting the remaining terms: \[\begin{align}
4E[S_{xx,i}S_{yy,i}]
&= 4\sigma_{xy}\bigl[2h_{x,i}^{(1)}h_{y,i}^{(1)} - h_{x,i}^{(1)}h_{y,i+1}^{(1)} - h_{x,i}^{(1)}h_{y,i}^{(2)} - h_{x,i+1}^{(1)}h_{y,i}^{(1)} + 2h_{x,i+1}^{(1)}h_{y,i+1}^{(1)} \\
&\qquad\quad - h_{x,i+1}^{(1)}h_{y,i}^{(2)} - h_{x,i}^{(2)}h_{y,i}^{(1)} - h_{x,i}^{(2)}h_{y,i+1}^{(1)} + 2h_{x,i}^{(2)}h_{y,i}^{(2)}\bigr] \\
&\quad + 4E[\varepsilon_x\varepsilon_y^2]\bigl(h_{x,i+1}^{(1)} - h_{x,i}^{(1)}\bigr) + 4E[\varepsilon_x^2\varepsilon_y]\bigl(h_{y,i+1}^{(1)} - h_{y,i}^{(1)}\bigr) \\
&\quad + 4\kappa_{22}\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 12\sigma_{xy}^2.
\end{align}\] Applying the linear identities \(h_{x,i}^{(1)} + h_{x,i+1}^{(1)} - h_{x,i}^{(2)} = 0\) and \(h_{y,i}^{(1)} + h_{y,i+1}^{(1)} - h_{y,i}^{(2)} = 0\) to substitute out \(h_{x,i}^{(2)}\) and \(h_{y,i}^{(2)}\) reduces the nine-term bracket to four terms: \[\begin{align}
4E[S_{xx,i}S_{yy,i}]
&= 4\sigma_{xy}\bigl[2h_{x,i}^{(1)}h_{y,i}^{(1)} - h_{x,i}^{(1)}h_{y,i+1}^{(1)} - h_{x,i+1}^{(1)}h_{y,i}^{(1)} + 2h_{x,i+1}^{(1)}h_{y,i+1}^{(1)}\bigr] \\
&\quad + 4E[\varepsilon_x\varepsilon_y^2]\bigl(h_{x,i+1}^{(1)} - h_{x,i}^{(1)}\bigr) + 4E[\varepsilon_x^2\varepsilon_y]\bigl(h_{y,i+1}^{(1)} - h_{y,i}^{(1)}\bigr) \\
&\quad + 4\kappa_{22}\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 12\sigma_{xy}^2.
\end{align}\]
Mixed-lag products vanish. The two cross terms \(h_{x,i}^{(1)}h_{y,i+1}^{(1)}\) and \(h_{x,i+1}^{(1)}h_{y,i}^{(1)}\) are identically zero at every index. Take the first: \(h_{x,i}^{(1)} = \theta_{x,i} - \theta_{x,i+1}\) is nonzero only if a change point falls in the gap \((i, i+1)\), while \(h_{y,i+1}^{(1)} = \theta_{y,i+1} - \theta_{y,i+2}\) is nonzero only if one falls in the adjacent gap \((i+1, i+2)\). Under common change-point locations, minimum segment length 2 forbids change points in adjacent gaps, so the two factors are never simultaneously nonzero and their product is \(0\). The same argument applies to \(h_{x,i+1}^{(1)}h_{y,i}^{(1)}\). The bracket collapses to two terms, and dividing by 4 gives \[\begin{align}
E[S_{xx,i}S_{yy,i}]
&= 2\sigma_{xy}\bigl(h_{x,i}^{(1)}h_{y,i}^{(1)} + h_{x,i+1}^{(1)}h_{y,i+1}^{(1)}\bigr) \\
&\quad + E[\varepsilon_x\varepsilon_y^2]\bigl(h_{x,i+1}^{(1)} - h_{x,i}^{(1)}\bigr) + E[\varepsilon_x^2\varepsilon_y]\bigl(h_{y,i+1}^{(1)} - h_{y,i}^{(1)}\bigr) \\
&\quad + \kappa_{22}\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 3\sigma_{xy}^2.
\end{align}\]
The signal-dependent terms make this index-varying, so \(E[S_{xx,i}S_{yy,i}] \neq \kappa_{22}\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2\) pointwise; it is the average \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_i S_{xx,i}S_{yy,i}\) that matters. Summing over \(i\), use that \(\sum_i h_{\cdot,i+1}^{(1)} = \sum_i h_{\cdot,i}^{(1)}\), since the two are rotations of each other. The coskewness terms then cancel, \[
\sum_i \bigl(h_{x,i+1}^{(1)} - h_{x,i}^{(1)}\bigr) = 0,
\] and the two covariance terms coincide, giving \[
\frac{1}{n}\sum_i E[S_{xx,i}S_{yy,i}] = \kappa_{22}\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 3\sigma_{xy}^2 + 4\sigma_{xy}\omega_{xy}.
\] Both bias terms \(3\sigma_{xy}^2\) and \(4\sigma_{xy}\omega_{xy}\) carry a factor of \(\sigma_{xy}\), so under \(H_0:\sigma_{xy}=0\) they vanish and \(\hat\kappa_{22}^{\mathrm{MoM}}\xrightarrow{p}\kappa_{22}\).

9.5.1 Estimating \(\kappa_{40}\)
Since \(\kappa_{22}(X,X) = E[\varepsilon_x^4]/\sigma_x^4 = \kappa_{40}\), the \(\kappa_{22}\) MoM estimator applies directly with \(Y = X\). Unlike the \(\kappa_{22}\) case where \(\sigma_{xy}\) is small under the null, here \(\sigma_{xy}\vert_{Y=X} = \sigma_x^2 \neq 0\), so the bias correction is non-trivial. Substituting \(\sigma_{xy} = \sigma_x^2\) into the \(\kappa_{22}\) consistency result gives \[\frac{1}{n}\sum_i E\bigl[S_{xx,i}^2\bigr] = \kappa_{40}\sigma_x^4 + 3\sigma_x^4 + 4\sigma_x^2\omega_{xx},\] so \[\hat\kappa_{40}^{\mathrm{MoM}} = \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_i S_{xx,i}^2 - 3\hat\sigma_x^4 - 4\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\omega_{xx}}{\hat\sigma_x^4}.\]






Consistency: \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_i S_{xx,i}^2 \xrightarrow{p} \kappa_{40}\sigma_x^4 + 3\sigma_x^4 + 4\sigma_x^2\omega_{xx}\)





Because \(\kappa_{40} = \kappa_{22}(X,X)\), we do not redo the four-case computation: we specialize the per-index master result of the \(\kappa_{22}\) consistency note to \(Y = X\). Under that substitution \(\sigma_y^2 \to \sigma_x^2\), \(\sigma_{xy} \to \sigma_x^2\), \(\kappa_{22} \to \kappa_{40}\), and both coskewnesses collapse to the skewness, \(E[\varepsilon_x\varepsilon_y^2], E[\varepsilon_x^2\varepsilon_y] \to \mu_3 := E[\varepsilon_x^3]\).
Pointwise mean. Setting \(Y = X\) in the per-index result \[E[S_{xx,i}S_{yy,i}] = 2\sigma_{xy}\bigl(h_{x,i}^{(1)}h_{y,i}^{(1)} + h_{x,i+1}^{(1)}h_{y,i+1}^{(1)}\bigr) + E[\varepsilon_x\varepsilon_y^2]\bigl(h_{x,i+1}^{(1)} - h_{x,i}^{(1)}\bigr) + E[\varepsilon_x^2\varepsilon_y]\bigl(h_{y,i+1}^{(1)} - h_{y,i}^{(1)}\bigr) + \kappa_{22}\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + 3\sigma_{xy}^2\] collapses the covariance bracket into a sum of squares: \[E\bigl[S_{xx,i}^2\bigr] = 2\sigma_x^2\bigl((h_i^{(1)})^2 + (h_{i+1}^{(1)})^2\bigr) + 2\mu_3\bigl(h_{i+1}^{(1)} - h_i^{(1)}\bigr) + (\kappa_{40} + 3)\sigma_x^4,\] writing \(h_i^{(k)} = \theta_{x,i} - \theta_{x,i+k}\).
Averaging over \(i\). Three pieces:

The skewness term telescopes. With circular indexing \(\sum_i h_{i+1}^{(1)} = \sum_i h_i^{(1)}\), so \(\sum_i 2\mu_3(h_{i+1}^{(1)} - h_i^{(1)}) = 0\).
The squared-jump terms each average to the signal-complexity functional \(\omega_{xx} := \frac{1}{n}\sum_i (h_i^{(1)})^2 \ge 0\) (again \(\sum_i (h_{i+1}^{(1)})^2 = \sum_i (h_i^{(1)})^2\) by rotation), contributing \(4\sigma_x^2\omega_{xx}\).
The constant survives as \((\kappa_{40}+3)\sigma_x^4\).

Hence \[\frac{1}{n}\sum_i E\bigl[S_{xx,i}^2\bigr] = \kappa_{40}\sigma_x^4 + 3\sigma_x^4 + 4\sigma_x^2\omega_{xx},\] which is the formula quoted above, now derived.
Why the bias does not vanish. In the \(\kappa_{22}\) case the bias \(3\sigma_{xy}^2 + 4\sigma_{xy}\omega_{xy}\) carried a factor of \(\sigma_{xy}\) and disappeared under \(H_0:\sigma_{xy}=0\). With \(Y=X\) there is no null to invoke: \(\sigma_{xy} = \sigma_x^2 \neq 0\). The \(3\sigma_x^4\) piece — arising because \(S_{xx,i}\) shares \(\varepsilon_{x,i+1}\) across its two factors — is an \(O(1)\) bias present at every sample size, while \(4\sigma_x^2\omega_{xx}\) is an \(O(L/n)\) signal bias (only the \(L\) change-point gaps contribute nonzero \(h_i^{(1)}\)). The estimator removes both explicitly through the \(-3\hat\sigma_x^4 - 4\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\omega_{xx}\) correction.
Convergence in probability. Each \(S_{xx,i}^2\) depends only on \((\varepsilon_{x,i}, \varepsilon_{x,i+1}, \varepsilon_{x,i+2})\), so the sequence is \(2\)-dependent; assuming finite eighth moments \(E[\varepsilon_x^8] < \infty\), the average has variance \(O(1/n) \to 0\), and by Chebyshev \[\frac{1}{n}\sum_i S_{xx,i}^2 \xrightarrow{p} \kappa_{40}\sigma_x^4 + 3\sigma_x^4 + 4\sigma_x^2\omega_{xx}.\] With \(\hat\sigma_x^2 \xrightarrow{p} \sigma_x^2\) and \(\hat\omega_{xx} \xrightarrow{p} \omega_{xx}\), the continuous mapping theorem gives \(\hat\kappa_{40}^{\mathrm{MoM}} \xrightarrow{p} \kappa_{40}\) — unconditionally, with no null hypothesis required.

Regression estimator and connection to quartic ECE terms





Define the quartic ECE terms \[S_{xx,i}^{(4)} = \frac{(X_i - X_{i+1})^4 + (X_{i+1} - X_{i+2})^4 - (X_i - X_{i+2})^4}{2}.\]
Write \(X_i - X_{i+k} = h_i^{(k)} + e_i^{(k)}\) where \(h_i^{(k)} = \theta_{x,i} - \theta_{x,i+k}\) and \(e_i^{(k)} = \varepsilon_{x,i} - \varepsilon_{x,i+k}\). Expanding: \[(h_i^{(k)} + e_i^{(k)})^4 = (h_i^{(k)})^4 + 4(h_i^{(k)})^3 e_i^{(k)} + 6(h_i^{(k)})^2(e_i^{(k)})^2 + 4h_i^{(k)}(e_i^{(k)})^3 + (e_i^{(k)})^4.\] Taking expectations, the odd cross-terms \(4(h_i^{(k)})^3 e_i^{(k)}\) and \(4h_i^{(k)}(e_i^{(k)})^3\) vanish: \(E[e_i^{(k)}] = 0\) trivially, and by iid (even for asymmetric distributions), \[E\bigl[(e_i^{(k)})^3\bigr] = E[\varepsilon_x^3] - E[\varepsilon_x^3] = 0.\] The remaining three groups each cancel:
Pure signal: \[(h_i^{(1)})^4 + (h_{i+1}^{(1)})^4 - (h_i^{(2)})^4 = 0\] by the change-point argument (min segment length 2 forces \(h_i^{(1)} = h_i^{(2)}\) and \(h_{i+1}^{(1)} = 0\), or vice versa).
Signal–noise cross term: \(E[6h^2 e^2] = 12\sigma_x^2(h_i^{(k)})^2\), so the combination gives \[(h_i^{(1)})^2 + (h_{i+1}^{(1)})^2 - (h_i^{(2)})^2 = 0\] by the quadratic ECE cancellation.
Pure noise: For any \(k \geq 1\), \(E[(e_i^{(k)})^4] = (2\kappa_{40}+6)\sigma_x^4\) by iid, so the combination gives \[\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl[(2\kappa_{40}+6) + (2\kappa_{40}+6) - (2\kappa_{40}+6)\bigr]\sigma_x^4 = (\kappa_{40}+3)\sigma_x^4.\]
Hence \(S_{xx,i}^{(4)}\) has constant mean at every index: \[E\bigl[S_{xx,i}^{(4)}\bigr] = (\kappa_{40}+3)\sigma_x^4.\]
The residual \(+3\) arises because \(S_{xx,i}\) shares \(\varepsilon_{x,i+1}\) across its two factors. Since \(S_{xx,i}\) and \(S_{xx,i+3}\) use non-overlapping observations, \(E[S_{xx,i}\cdot S_{xx,i+3}] = \sigma_x^4\) at every index. Subtracting three times this lag-3 product gives constant mean \(\kappa_{40}\sigma_x^4\): \[\hat\kappa_{40}^{\mathrm{MoM}} = \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_i \bigl[S_{xx,i}^{(4)} - 3\,S_{xx,i}\,S_{xx,i+3}\bigr]}{\bar S_{xx}^2}.\]
With circular indexing \(\sum_i S_{xx,i}^{(4)} = (2T_1^{(2)}(X,X) - T_2^{(2)}(X,X))/2\), so this is algebraically identical to the regression formula above when \(\tfrac{1}{n}\sum S_{xx,i}S_{xx,i+3}\) is replaced by \(\bar S_{xx}^2\).
