9.5.2 Estimating \(\kappa_{31}\)
As with \(\kappa_{22}\), there are two routes to \(\kappa_{31} = E[\varepsilon_x^3\varepsilon_y]/(\sigma_x^3\sigma_y)\): a regression estimator built from a single fourth-order ECE term, and a method-of-moments estimator built from a product of two second-order ECE terms. The regression term cancels the change-point signal exactly and needs only a \(3\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_{xy}\) correction; the MoM has the lower variance (the \(\kappa_{22}\) comparison note) but its product retains change-point complexity terms that must also be subtracted.
Regression estimator. Define the cubic-linear ECE term \[T_i = \frac{t_i^{(1)} + t_{i+1}^{(1)} - t_i^{(2)}}{2}, \qquad t_i^{(k)} = (X_i - X_{i+k})^3(Y_i - Y_{i+k}).\] The change-point cancellation gives constant mean at every index, \(E[T_i] = \kappa_{31}\sigma_x^3\sigma_y + 3\sigma_x^2\sigma_{xy}\), so \[\hat\kappa_{31}^{\mathrm{reg}} = \frac{\bar T - 3\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_{xy}}{\bar S_{xx}^{3/2}\,\bar S_{yy}^{1/2}}.\]
Method of moments. Factor \(\varepsilon_x^3\varepsilon_y = \varepsilon_x^2\cdot(\varepsilon_x\varepsilon_y)\) and replace each factor by its second-order ECE surrogate: \(S_{xx,i}\) for \(\varepsilon_x^2\) (mean \(\sigma_x^2\) at every index) and \(S_{xy,i}\) for \(\varepsilon_x\varepsilon_y\) (mean \(\sigma_{xy}\) at every index). Their product is a surrogate for \(\varepsilon_x^3\varepsilon_y\). Replacing the single quartic term \(T_i\) by this product lowers the variance (the \(\kappa_{22}\) comparison note), but unlike \(T_i\) — whose signal cancels exactly at every index — the product carries two change-point complexity terms, \(\omega_{xx} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i (h_{x,i}^{(1)})^2\) and \(\omega_{xy} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i h_{x,i}^{(1)}h_{y,i}^{(1)}\) (with \(h_{x,i}^{(1)} = \theta_{x,i} - \theta_{x,i+1}\)). Subtracting these alongside the \(3\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_{xy}\) bias (proof below), \[\hat\kappa_{31}^{\mathrm{MoM}} = \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_i S_{xx,i}\,S_{xy,i} - 3\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_{xy} - 2\hat\sigma_{xy}\hat\omega_{xx} - 2\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\omega_{xy}}{\bar S_{xx}^{3/2}\,\bar S_{yy}^{1/2}},\] where \(\hat\omega_{xx}\) and \(\hat\omega_{xy}\) are the ECE complexity estimates ece.complexity(x, x) and ece.complexity(x, y).






Consistency: \(\frac{1}{n}\sum_i S_{xx,i}S_{xy,i} \xrightarrow{p} \kappa_{31}\sigma_x^3\sigma_y + 3\sigma_x^2\sigma_{xy} + 2\sigma_{xy}\omega_{xx} + 2\sigma_x^2\omega_{xy}\)





Surrogates and the general term. Split each increment into signal and noise, \(X_i - X_{i+k} = h_{x,i}^{(k)} + e_{x,i}^{(k)}\) and \(Y_i - Y_{i+k} = h_{y,i}^{(k)} + e_{y,i}^{(k)}\). With \(s_{xx,i}^{(k)} = (X_i-X_{i+k})^2\) and \(s_{xy,i}^{(k)} = (X_i-X_{i+k})(Y_i-Y_{i+k})\), \[S_{xx,i} = \tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(s_{xx,i}^{(1)} + s_{xx,i+1}^{(1)} - s_{xx,i}^{(2)}\bigr), \qquad S_{xy,i} = \tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(s_{xy,i}^{(1)} + s_{xy,i+1}^{(1)} - s_{xy,i}^{(2)}\bigr).\] The product expands into nine cross terms; it suffices to analyze the general term \(E[s_{xx,i}^{(k)}\,s_{xy,j}^{(r)}] = E[a^2 b c]\) with \(a = X_i - X_{i+k}\), \(b = X_j - X_{j+r}\), \(c = Y_j - Y_{j+r}\). Substituting the signal–noise split and using \(E[e]=0\) separates this into a pure-noise part \(E[(e_{x,i}^{(k)})^2 e_{x,j}^{(r)} e_{y,j}^{(r)}]\) plus terms each carrying at least one signal factor \(h\).
Pure-noise baseline. The pure-noise term depends only on how the index sets \(\{i,i+k\}\) and \(\{j,j+r\}\) overlap. The three diagonal combinations (matching index and lag) share both time points, where \[E\bigl[(e_x^{(k)})^3 e_y^{(k)}\bigr] = 2\kappa_{31}\sigma_x^3\sigma_y + 6\sigma_x^2\sigma_{xy};\] each of the six off-diagonal combinations shares exactly one time point and evaluates to \(\kappa_{31}\sigma_x^3\sigma_y + 3\sigma_x^2\sigma_{xy}\). Assembling with the ECE signs \((s_{xx,i}^{(1)} + s_{xx,i+1}^{(1)} - s_{xx,i}^{(2)})(s_{xy,i}^{(1)} + s_{xy,i+1}^{(1)} - s_{xy,i}^{(2)})\) — the three diagonal terms enter with \(+\), the six off-diagonal terms with net sign \(2(+) + 4(-) = -2\) — \[4\,E[S_{xx,i}S_{xy,i}]_{\text{noise}} = 3\bigl(2\kappa_{31}\sigma_x^3\sigma_y + 6\sigma_x^2\sigma_{xy}\bigr) - 2\bigl(\kappa_{31}\sigma_x^3\sigma_y + 3\sigma_x^2\sigma_{xy}\bigr) = 4\kappa_{31}\sigma_x^3\sigma_y + 12\sigma_x^2\sigma_{xy},\] so the pure-noise part has constant mean \(\kappa_{31}\sigma_x^3\sigma_y + 3\sigma_x^2\sigma_{xy}\) at every index — exactly the regression estimator’s target and bias.
Signal-dependent terms. The remaining terms each carry a signal factor \(h\). The pure-signal quartic cancels exactly (the min-segment-length-2 argument of the \(\kappa_{40}\) note), and the terms linear in a single \(h\) telescope to zero under circular rotation (as in the \(\kappa_{22}\) note). The surviving signal\(^2\times\)noise\(^2\) terms collect into two change-point complexity functionals, \[2\sigma_{xy}\,\omega_{xx} + 2\sigma_x^2\,\omega_{xy}, \qquad \omega_{xx} = \tfrac{1}{n}\textstyle\sum_i (h_{x,i}^{(1)})^2, \quad \omega_{xy} = \tfrac{1}{n}\textstyle\sum_i h_{x,i}^{(1)} h_{y,i}^{(1)}.\] Note \(\omega_{xy}\) carries no factor of \(\sigma_{xy}\), so it biases the estimator even under independence; the regression term \(T_i\), which cancels the signal pointwise, has no such terms.
Averaged mean and consistency. Collecting the pieces, \[\frac{1}{n}\sum_i E[S_{xx,i}S_{xy,i}] = \kappa_{31}\sigma_x^3\sigma_y + 3\sigma_x^2\sigma_{xy} + 2\sigma_{xy}\omega_{xx} + 2\sigma_x^2\omega_{xy}.\] Each \(S_{xx,i}S_{xy,i}\) depends only on \((\varepsilon_{\cdot,i}, \varepsilon_{\cdot,i+1}, \varepsilon_{\cdot,i+2})\), so the sequence is \(2\)-dependent; with finite eighth moments the average has variance \(O(1/n)\) and concentrates at its mean. All four bias terms are estimated consistently — \(\hat\sigma_x^2 = \bar S_{xx}\), \(\hat\sigma_{xy} = \bar S_{xy}\), and \(\hat\omega_{xx}, \hat\omega_{xy}\) by the ECE complexity regression (ece.complexity) — so subtracting them and normalizing, \[\hat\kappa_{31}^{\mathrm{MoM}} = \frac{\frac{1}{n}\sum_i S_{xx,i}S_{xy,i} - 3\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\sigma_{xy} - 2\hat\sigma_{xy}\hat\omega_{xx} - 2\hat\sigma_x^2\hat\omega_{xy}}{\bar S_{xx}^{3/2}\,\bar S_{yy}^{1/2}} \xrightarrow{p} \kappa_{31}\] by the continuous mapping theorem. As with \(\kappa_{40}\), the change-point complexity terms are subtracted explicitly; the regression estimator avoids them only because its quartic term cancels the signal pointwise.

9.7 Numerical Results: Estimating \(\kappa_{22}\)
The MoM estimator has lower variance than both the regression and covariance estimators across scenarios. Between regression and covariance, neither dominates: regression wins in low-amplitude settings, covariance wins when change-point amplitude is large.










Regression DominatesCovariance Dominates































Why does MoM have lower variance than the regression estimator?



The regression estimator computes a single fourth-order joint statistic \(T_k^{(2)} = \sum_i (X_i - X_{i+k})^2(Y_i - Y_{i+k})^2\), whereas the MoM builds separate second-order estimates \(S_{xx,i} \approx \sigma_x^2\) and \(S_{yy,i} \approx \sigma_y^2\) and multiplies them. Since \(\kappa_{22}\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 = E[\varepsilon_x^2\varepsilon_y^2]\) factors, this separation pays off: for independent estimates \(\hat A, \hat B\) of \(A, B\), \[\operatorname{Var}[\hat A \hat B] \approx A^2\operatorname{Var}[\hat B] + B^2\operatorname{Var}[\hat A] \leq \operatorname{Var}[\widehat{AB}].\]
Near a joint change point the advantage is even larger: \((X_i - X_{i+k})^2(Y_i - Y_{i+k})^2 \sim h_x^2 h_y^2\) is fourth-order in jump amplitudes, while \(S_{xx,i} S_{yy,i}\) is only quadratic (the signal’s squared term cancels inside each ECE term), so the regression numerator is far noisier in high-amplitude scenarios.

10.1 Generating Correlated Errors via Cholesky Decomposition
To simulate errors with a target covariance matrix \(\Sigma\), we use the Cholesky decomposition. Factor \(\Sigma = L^T L\) where \(L\) is upper triangular. Then for any \(n \times p\) matrix \(Z\) with iid entries of mean zero and unit variance,
\[
E = Z L
\]
has \(\text{Cov}(E_t) = L^T \text{Cov}(Z_t) L = L^T L = \Sigma\).
In generate_err, \(L\) = chol(S) and the correlated errors are produced as Z %*% chol(S). The marginal distribution of each entry of \(Z\) — normal, \(t\), log-normal, etc. — determines the marginal distribution of \(\varepsilon_t\), while the covariance structure is always \(\Sigma\) regardless of that choice.

11.3 \(p = 2\): Dependence Testing (Quadratic)
Correlation dependence testing are closely related but subtly different. In the classical Pearson test, interpretation is dependent on on the assumptions made.
Consider this canonical example: \[
\varepsilon_y = \frac{\varepsilon_x^2 - 1}{\sqrt{2}}, \quad
\varepsilon_x \sim N(0, 1).
\] Clearly, \(\varepsilon_x\) and \(\varepsilon_y\) are dependent, but by construction \(\operatorname{Cor}(\varepsilon_x, \varepsilon_y) = 0\). Specifically, \(\kappa_{22} = 5\).
Therefore, a dependence test will identify dependence between \(\varepsilon_x\) and \(\varepsilon_y\), but a correlation test will not.

title: 11  Type I Error
text:
11.4 \(p = 2:\) Dependence Testing (\(\kappa_{22} = 0.5\))
The case \(\kappa_{22} < 1\) is a bit unnatural. For bivariate Gaussian errors, \[\kappa_{22} = 1 + 2\rho^2 \geq 1 \text{ for all } \rho \in [-1, 1],\] so the Gaussian family can never produce it.
Since \[\kappa_{22} = 1 + \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_x^2, \varepsilon_y^2)}{\sigma_x^2 \sigma_y^2},\] having \(\kappa_{22} < 1\) requires \(\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_x^2, \varepsilon_y^2) < 0\): large squared values of one component must tend to coincide with small squared values of the other.
The circular distribution provides a concrete construction: \[
U \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0, 2\pi), \quad
\varepsilon_x = \sqrt{2}\cos(U), \quad
\varepsilon_y = \sqrt{2}\sin(U).
\] Because \(\varepsilon_x^2 + \varepsilon_y^2 = 2\) almost surely, whenever \(\varepsilon_x^2\) is large \(\varepsilon_y^2\) must be small, giving exactly the required negative covariance: \(\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_x^2, \varepsilon_y^2) = \mathbb{E}[\sin^2(2U)] - 1 = \tfrac{1}{2} - 1 = -\tfrac{1}{2}\). With \(\sigma_x^2 = \sigma_y^2 = 1\), this yields \(\kappa_{22} = 0.5\).
At the same time, \(\operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_x, \varepsilon_y) = \mathbb{E}[\sin(2U)] = 0\), so the errors are uncorrelated and a Pearson correlation test has no power — yet the pair is strongly dependent.

11.9.3 Mechanism: Not in Asymptotic CLT Regime
The u-shaped p-curves indicate that there are insufficient small and large p-values. This means the distribution of bootstrap statistics has less variance than the true distribution.
To see why, we compare the distribution of the test statistic \(Q = \max_j |\bar S_j|\) under two distributions. The true distribution is obtained by repeatedly drawing a fresh dataset and computing \(Q\) from the observed \(\bar S\). The bootstrap distribution is obtained by drawing a single dataset, estimating the covariance \(W\) of \(\bar S\) from that dataset, and then drawing one bootstrap replicate \(Q^* = \max_j |Z_j|\) with \(Z \sim N(0, W)\). When \(n\) is small relative to \(p\), \(W\) underestimates the true variance of \(\bar S\), so the bootstrap distribution is too narrow and the test is conservative.
The plots below also include four related distributions:

True: the actual distribution of the test statistic, obtained by repeatedly generating a fresh dataset and computing \(Q\) directly, with no covariance estimation involved — this is the ground truth the others are compared against.
Bootstrap: for each simulated dataset, we estimate \(W\) from that dataset and draw a single bootstrap replicate \(Q^*\) from \(N(0, W)\). This differs from how the bootstrap is used in practice, where we would draw many replicates from the same estimated \(W\) to build a reference distribution for a single dataset’s test; here we draw only one replicate per dataset so that repeating this many times traces out the bootstrap’s overall sampling distribution.
Bootstrap (Oracle): replaces the single-sample estimate of \(W\) with its true value (found by averaging over many datasets), isolating whether the conservativeness comes from estimating \(W\) or is inherent to the method.
Naive Bootstrap: estimates \(W\) using the ordinary sample covariance, which is only valid when there are no change points; it serves as a benchmark for the upper bound on performance.
Naive Bootstrap (Oracle): the oracle version of the naive estimate.

title: 13  CO2 Inhalation
text:
13.1 Bootstrap Methods
De Roover et al. (2014) collect physiological data from an individual over time. The individual wears a gas mask that allows the user to breathe regular air or a \(CO_2\) mixture. He is asked to breathe normally throughout the course of the experiment while the experimenters discretely change the air mixture. This induces three experimental states:
With each breath, they record respiratory data such as the length of inhalation (Ti), length of exhalation (Te), and the total length of the respiratory cycle (Tt = Ti + Te). They also record cardiac data such as heart rate (HR) and the cardiac interbeat interval (RR) — the time between peaks on an electrocardiogram. Together, this forms a time series where each index represents a breath.
This dataset is useful because there are experimentally induced change points. The data itself contains information on when different phases of the experiment occur. Having known change points makes it possible to compare the segmentation method, which explicitly adjusts for the mean shifts, against ECE, which only implicitly adjusts for them. Ideally, both methods produce similar results. Moreover, we know the direction of some correlations a priori. For example, HR and RR are inversely related: a higher heart rate corresponds to a shorter distance between R-peaks on an electrocardiogram. And since Tt = Ti + Te, we expect Ti and Te to both correlate with Tt.
In total, they collect 290 data points. However, the subject’s movement may incur measurement error, so they remove an additional 51 observations, leaving a total of 239 data points. Finally, they normalize each time series to have mean zero and unit variance. We access this data directly from the kcpRS R package (Cabrieto et al., 2022).
Variables:
Figure 1 shows the respiratory time series. The respiratory times decrease with the introduction of \(CO_2\) and partially recover afterward. Figure 2 shows the cardiac series; heart rate and interbeat interval move in opposite directions, consistent with their known inverse relationship.
Both methods correctly identify the block-diagonal structure: Ti, Te, and Tt are mutually correlated, and HR and RR are negatively correlated. However, both methods detect a significant correlation between Tt and HR in opposite directions. To understand which is correct, we refer to oracle segmentation. The data as a whole does not show strong variation across experimental phases in the off-diagonal block, suggesting neither method has a clear advantage here.
This application is a reminder that even when the times experimental conditions change are known, it may be insufficient to fully remove the corresponding mean shifts. The changes in this dataset appear gradual rather than abrupt, which challenges the assumptions of both the segmentation and change-point models.

bartlett_diag_test <- function(X) {
  n <- nrow(X)
  R <- cor(X)
  p <- ncol(X)
  q <- p * (p - 1) / 2

  # Chi-squared statistic: -(n-1) * log(det(R))
  chi2 <- -(n - 1) * log(det(R))
  p_val <- pchisq(chi2, df = q, lower.tail = FALSE)

  list(statistic = chi2, df = q, p.value = p_val)
}

title: 17  Positive Semidefinite
text:
17.1 Existence of an Unbiased PSD Estimator
The ECE is not guaranteed to be positive semidefinite. In particular, when applied to estimate a variance (\(X = Y\)), the estimator \(\hat{\sigma}_{xx} = X^T A X\) can return negative values, since the matrix \(A\) itself is not positive semidefinite.
If \(A \succeq 0\) and \(\theta_x^T A \theta_y = 0\) for all \(\theta_x, \theta_y \in \Theta_L\), then in particular \(\theta^T A \theta = 0\) for all \(\theta \in \Theta_L\). Since \(A \succeq 0\), all eigenvalues are non-negative. Using the eigendecomposition \(A = Q\Lambda Q^*\) with \(\lambda_j \geq 0\),
\[\theta^T A \theta = \sum_j \lambda_j |\tilde\theta_j|^2 = 0.\]
Since every term is non-negative, each must vanish individually: \(\lambda_j |\tilde\theta_j|^2 = 0\) for all \(j\), so \(\lambda_j \tilde\theta_j = 0\) for all \(j\). Therefore \(A\theta = Q\Lambda\tilde\theta = 0\). This shows that any unbiased PSD estimator must satisfy \(A\theta = 0\) for all \(\theta \in \Theta_L\). If \(\operatorname{span}(\Theta_L) = \mathbb{R}^n\), this forces \(A = 0\), contradicting \(\operatorname{tr}(A) = 1\). Whether \(\Theta_L\) spans \(\mathbb{R}^n\) depends on \(n\) and \(L\) and is not established here.

title: 17  Positive Semidefinite
text:
17.2 PSD Projection via Eigenvalue Clipping
The closest positive semidefinite matrix to \(A\) in Frobenius norm is obtained by replacing negative eigenvalues with zero. Given the eigendecomposition \(A = Q\Lambda Q^*\), define
\[\Lambda_+ = \operatorname{diag}(\max(\lambda_0, 0), \ldots, \max(\lambda_{n-1}, 0))\]
and form
\[A_+ = Q\Lambda_+ Q^*.\]
The resulting estimator \(\hat{\sigma}_{xy}^+ = X^T A_+ Y\) is guaranteed to be non-negative when \(X = Y\), since \(A_+ \succeq 0\). The cost is that \(A_+\) no longer satisfies the unbiasedness constraints.

title: 17  Positive Semidefinite
section: 17.3 Bias Analysis of the PSD Projection
text:
17.3 Bias Analysis of the PSD Projection
The bias of \(\hat{\sigma}_{xy}^+ = X^T A_+ Y\) is
\[
\mathbb{E}[\hat{\sigma}_{xy}^+] = \theta_x^T A_+ \theta_y + \sigma_{xy} \operatorname{tr}(A_+).
\]
By clipping negative eigenvalues, we have \(\operatorname{tr}(A_+) = \sum_{j: \lambda_j \geq 0} \lambda_j < \operatorname{tr}(A) = 1\). The bias is therefore
\[
\text{Bias}(A_+) = \theta_x^T A_+ \theta_y + \sigma_{xy} \left(\operatorname{tr}(A_+) - 1\right).
\]
The second term \(\sigma_{xy}(\operatorname{tr}(A_+) - 1)\) is always negative (when \(\sigma_{xy} > 0\)), introducing systematic downward bias. By clipping, we lose the negative eigenvalue contributions that canceled the positive ones under correct specification. For \(\theta_x, \theta_y \in \Theta_L\), the original cancellation \(\sum_j \lambda_j |\tilde\theta_j|^2 = 0\) becomes a non-cancellation \(\sum_j \lambda_j^+ |\tilde\theta_j|^2 \geq 0\) after clipping, introducing an additional positive spectral bias. The total bias is thus driven by both the trace loss and the broken cancellation, and its magnitude depends on the size and location of the negative eigenvalues in the spectrum.

title: 18  Model Misspecification
text:
18.1 Key Concepts
The signal \(\theta\). A vector \((\theta_0, \ldots, \theta_{n-1})\) where \(\theta_i\) is the true mean of the time series at time \(i\). The ECE is designed for piecewise-constant \(\theta\); misspecification means \(\theta\) has some other shape.
Frequency index \(j\). An integer from \(0\) to \(n-1\) labeling a sinusoidal component. Specifically, \(j\) counts how many complete oscillations the sinusoid \(\cos(2\pi j i / n)\) makes as \(i\) runs from \(0\) to \(n-1\):
The plot below shows what each of these looks like concretely.
The DFT. The Discrete Fourier Transform rewrites \(\theta\) as a sum of sinusoids — one at each frequency \(j\). The complex coefficient \(\tilde\theta_j\) says how much of \(\theta\) oscillates at rate \(j\).
Energy \(|\tilde\theta_j|^2/n\). How much of \(\theta\)’s total variation comes from frequency \(j\). A tall bar at \(j = 5\) means \(\theta\) has a strong 5-cycle-per-window oscillation. By Parseval’s theorem, the energies sum to \(\|\theta\|^2/n\).
Eigenvalues \(\lambda_j\). The ECE matrix \(A\) acts differently on each frequency: it scales sinusoidal components by \(\lambda_j\). Small \(|\lambda_j|\) means the ECE ignores energy at that frequency; large \(|\lambda_j|\) means energy there leaks into the bias.
The bias formula. Because of the eigendecomposition \(A = Q\Lambda Q^*\), the bias simplifies to a frequency-by-frequency weighted sum:
\[\theta^T A \theta = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} \lambda_j \cdot \frac{|\tilde\theta_j|^2}{n}\]
This is the central formula for understanding misspecification: the bias is the dot product between the signal’s energy profile and the ECE’s frequency sensitivity. Wherever \(\lambda_j \approx 0\), that frequency contributes nothing to the bias regardless of how much energy \(\theta\) places there.

text:

title: 18  Model Misspecification
text:
18.2 Circulant Matrices and the DFT
Every symmetric circulant \(A = \operatorname{circ}(a)\) is diagonalized by the DFT matrix \(F \in \mathbb{C}^{n \times n}\),
\[
A = F^* \Lambda F,
\]
where \(F_{jk} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \omega^{jk}\), \(\omega = e^{-2\pi i/n}\), and \(\Lambda = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_0, \ldots, \lambda_{n-1})\). The eigenvalues are the DFT of the first row:
\[
\lambda_j = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k\, \omega^{jk} = (\mathcal{F} a)_j.
\]
Since \(A\) is real and symmetric, the eigenvalues are real and satisfy \(\lambda_j = \lambda_{n-j}\).
Because \(F\) is unitary (\(F F^* = I\)), the decomposition \(A = F^* \Lambda F\) is exactly the eigendecomposition \(A = Q \Lambda Q^{-1}\) with \(Q = F^*\). The columns of \(F^*\) are the eigenvectors of \(A\): the \(j\)-th eigenvector is \(f_j = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}(1, \omega^{-j}, \omega^{-2j}, \ldots, \omega^{-(n-1)j})^T\), a complex sinusoid at frequency \(j/n\).






DFT and eigendecomposition are the same thing for circulants

  QD <- Q %*% diag(fft(a) / n)  # eigenvalues = fft(a)/n for scaled A
  expect_equal(Re(AQ), Re(QD), tolerance = 1e-10)
  expect_equal(Im(AQ), Im(QD), tolerance = 1e-10)
})

Test passed 😸





Spectral representation of the bias. Using the eigendecomposition \(A = Q\Lambda Q^*\) with \(Q = F^*\),
\[
\theta_x^T A \theta_y = \theta_x^T Q \Lambda Q^* \theta_y = (Q^*\theta_x)^* \Lambda (Q^*\theta_y) = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} \lambda_j\, \tilde{\theta}_{x,j}^*\, \tilde{\theta}_{y,j},
\]
where \(\tilde{\theta} = Q^*\theta\) are the coordinates of \(\theta\) in the eigenbasis.
Under correct specification (\(\theta \in \Theta_L\)), the \(j = 0\) term vanishes because \(\lambda_0 = 0\) always — the DC eigenvalue is zero since \(\sum_k a_k = 0\) by the block-sum constraints. For \(j > 0\), neither \(\lambda_j\) nor \(\tilde{\theta}_j\) is zero in general; the sum cancels through structured pairwise cancellation across frequencies, a consequence of the block-sum constraints rather than anything visible in \(\lambda\) or \(\tilde{\theta}\) individually.
The spectral representation is most useful under misspecification. When \(\theta \notin \Theta_L\), the pairwise cancellation breaks down and the bias
\[
\theta_x^T A \theta_y = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} \lambda_j\, \tilde{\theta}_{x,j}^*\, \tilde{\theta}_{y,j}
\]
is nonzero. Its magnitude depends on which eigenvalues \(\lambda_j\) are large and how much energy \(\tilde{\theta}_x\), \(\tilde{\theta}_y\) place at the corresponding frequencies.

title: 18  Model Misspecification
text:
18.3 Closed-Form Bias
Since \(A = \sum_{k=1}^L c_k A_k\) with \(c_k = H_{1,k} = \frac{2L+1-3k}{nL(L-1)}\) (see Other Mathematical Results), the bias decomposes as
\[
\theta_x^T A \theta_y = \sum_{k=1}^L c_k\, T_k(\theta_x, \theta_y),
\]
where \(T_k(\theta_x, \theta_y) = \sum_{i=1}^n (\theta_{x,i} - \theta_{x,i+k})(\theta_{y,i} - \theta_{y,i+k})\) is the \(k\)-lagged cross-product of the mean vectors. For \(L = 2\) this reduces to
\[
\theta_x^T A \theta_y = \frac{1}{2n}\bigl(2T_1(\theta_x, \theta_y) - T_2(\theta_x, \theta_y)\bigr).
\]
Spectral form of \(\lambda_j\). Applying the eigendecomposition of \(A_k\) — whose eigenvalues are \(4\sin^2(\pi jk/n)\) — gives a closed form for the eigenvalues of \(A\):
\[
\lambda_j = \sum_{k=1}^L c_k \cdot 4\sin^2\!\left(\frac{\pi jk}{n}\right) = \frac{4}{nL(L-1)}\sum_{k=1}^L (2L+1-3k)\sin^2\!\left(\frac{\pi jk}{n}\right).
\]
For \(L = 2\) this simplifies to
\[
\lambda_j = -\frac{4}{n}\cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi j}{n}\right)\sin^2\!\left(\frac{\pi j}{n}\right).
\]
Bias bound. By Cauchy–Schwarz in the eigenbasis, and using \(\|\tilde{\theta}\|_2 = \|\theta\|_2\) (unitarity of \(Q\)),
\[
|\theta_x^T A \theta_y| \leq \max_j |\lambda_j| \cdot \|\theta_x\|_2 \|\theta_y\|_2.
\]
The bias is therefore controlled by \(\max_j |\lambda_j|\), which from the \(L=2\) formula is largest near the Nyquist frequency \(j = n/2\). Misspecification is most harmful when the mean vectors have energy concentrated at high frequencies.

title: 18  Model Misspecification
text:
18.4 Closed-Form Variance
The variance of \(X^T A Y\) is (see the Bilinear Form chapter):
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X^T A Y) = \sigma_y^2\,\theta_x^T A^2 \theta_x + \sigma_x^2\,\theta_y^T A^2 \theta_y + 2\sigma_{xy}\,\theta_x^T A^2 \theta_y + (\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + \sigma_{xy}^2)\operatorname{tr}(A^2).
\]
The noise term \((\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + \sigma_{xy}^2)\operatorname{tr}(A^2) = O(1/n)\) regardless of the mean. The signal-dependent terms involve \(\theta_x^T A^2 \theta_y\), which mirrors the bias with \(A\) replaced by \(A^2\).
Spectral form. Since \(A^2 = Q\Lambda^2 Q^*\),
\[
\theta_x^T A^2 \theta_y = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} \lambda_j^2\, \tilde{\theta}_{x,j}^*\, \tilde{\theta}_{y,j},
\]
where \(\tilde{\theta} = Q^*\theta\). This is the spectral bias formula with \(\lambda_j\) replaced by \(\lambda_j^2\).
Spectral form of \(\lambda_j^2\). For \(L = 2\), squaring \(\lambda_j = -\frac{4}{n}\cos(2\pi j/n)\sin^2(\pi j/n)\):
\[
\lambda_j^2 = \frac{16}{n^2}\cos^2\!\left(\frac{2\pi j}{n}\right)\sin^4\!\left(\frac{\pi j}{n}\right).
\]
Variance bound. By Cauchy–Schwarz in the eigenbasis:
\[
|\theta_x^T A^2 \theta_y| \leq \max_j \lambda_j^2 \cdot \|\theta_x\|_2 \|\theta_y\|_2 = \left(\max_j |\lambda_j|\right)^2 \|\theta_x\|_2 \|\theta_y\|_2.
\]
The signal-dependent variance is controlled by the same Nyquist-dominated \(\max_j|\lambda_j|\) as the bias.

title: 18  Model Misspecification
text:
18.5 Case Study: Sinusoidal Mean
Suppose \(\theta_x = \theta_y = \theta\) with \(\theta_i = A\sin(2\pi fi/n)\) for integer frequency \(1 \leq f < n/2\) and amplitude \(A > 0\). This is misspecified since a sinusoid is not piecewise constant.

18.5.1 Bias
Computing \(T_k(\theta, \theta)\). Applying the sum-to-product identity \(\sin\alpha - \sin\beta = 2\cos\!\left(\frac{\alpha+\beta}{2}\right)\sin\!\left(\frac{\alpha-\beta}{2}\right)\),
\[
\theta_i - \theta_{i+k} = -2A\sin\!\left(\frac{\pi fk}{n}\right)\cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi fi}{n} + \frac{\pi fk}{n}\right).
\]
Squaring and summing over \(i\), and using \(\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\cos^2(\alpha + 2\pi fi/n) = n/2\) for \(f \neq 0\),
\[
T_k(\theta, \theta) = 2nA^2\sin^2\!\left(\frac{\pi fk}{n}\right).
\]
Bias for \(L = 2\). Substituting into \(\frac{1}{2n}(2T_1 - T_2)\),
\[
\theta^T A \theta = 2A^2\sin^2\!\left(\frac{\pi f}{n}\right) - A^2\sin^2\!\left(\frac{2\pi f}{n}\right).
\]
Using \(\sin^2(2\phi) = 4\sin^2(\phi)\cos^2(\phi)\) and the double-angle identity \(1 - 2\cos^2\phi = -\cos(2\phi)\),
\[
\theta^T A \theta = -2A^2\sin^2\!\left(\frac{\pi f}{n}\right)\cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi f}{n}\right).
\]
Interpretation. The bias depends on frequency and amplitude but not on phase. It is zero at \(f = 0\) (constant — well specified) and at \(f = n/4\) (where \(\cos(2\pi f/n) = 0\)), negative for \(f < n/4\), and positive for \(f > n/4\). It grows as \(A^2\) and is largest near the Nyquist frequency \(f = n/2\), consistent with the general bound \(|\text{bias}| \leq \max_j|\lambda_j| \cdot \|\theta\|_2^2\).

Application to scenario 14. Scenario 14 sets \(\theta_i = \sin(2\pi i / 365)\) — a yearly cycle sampled at daily resolution. With \(n = 100\) observations, the signal has effective DFT bin \(j \approx n/365 \approx 0.27\), well below \(j = 1\). Since \(\lambda_j \approx 0\) near \(j = 0\), the formula predicts negligible bias: \(|\text{bias}| \approx 2\sin^2(\pi/365) \approx 1.5 \times 10^{-4}\) per unit amplitude squared. Numerically the bias is of order \(10^{-5}\), confirming that the ECE is effectively unbiased in this scenario despite the misspecification — the yearly cycle is too slow relative to the observation window to contaminate the estimate.
With \(n = 1000\) observations, the window covers approximately 2.7 full periods and the effective bin shifts to \(j \approx 2.74\). The bias is now \(\approx -1.6 \times 10^{-4}\) — negative since \(j < n/4 = 250\), and consistent with the formula prediction of \(-1.5 \times 10^{-4}\). Despite the larger signal (\(\|\theta\|^2 \approx 499\)), the bias remains negligible: the yearly cycle is still low-frequency relative to \(n\).


18.5.2 Variance
With \(\theta_x = \theta_y = \theta\), the closed-form variance simplifies to
\[\operatorname{Var}(X^T A Y) = (\sigma_x^2 + \sigma_y^2 + 2\sigma_{xy})\,\theta^T A^2 \theta + (\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + \sigma_{xy}^2)\operatorname{tr}(A^2).\]
Computing \(\theta^T A^2 \theta\). Since \(\theta_i = A\sin(2\pi fi/n)\) lies in the eigenspace of \(A\) at frequency \(f\) and \(\lambda_f = \lambda_{n-f}\), we have \(A\theta = \lambda_f\,\theta\). Therefore \(\theta^T A^2 \theta = \lambda_f^2\|\theta\|^2 = \frac{nA^2}{2}\lambda_f^2\).
For \(L = 2\). Substituting the \(L=2\) eigenvalue:
\[\operatorname{Var}(X^T A Y) = \frac{8A^2}{n}(\sigma_x^2 + \sigma_y^2 + 2\sigma_{xy})\cos^2\!\left(\frac{2\pi f}{n}\right)\sin^4\!\left(\frac{\pi f}{n}\right) + (\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + \sigma_{xy}^2)\operatorname{tr}(A^2).\]
Both terms are \(O(1/n)\). The signal-dependent term vanishes at the same frequencies as the bias (\(f = 0\) and \(f = n/4\)).

title: 18  Model Misspecification
text:
18.6 Case Study: Random Walk Mean
Suppose \(\theta_x = \theta_y = \theta\) where \(\theta_i = \sum_{j=1}^i \xi_j\) is a random walk with i.i.d. increments \(\xi_j \sim (0, \sigma^2)\). This corresponds to scenario 13.
Expected bias is \(O(1/n)\). Since \(\theta_i - \theta_{i+k} = \xi_{i+1} + \cdots + \xi_{i+k}\) is a sum of \(k\) independent increments,
\[
E\bigl[(\theta_i - \theta_{i+k})^2\bigr] = k\sigma^2,
\]






Why \(E[(\theta_i - \theta_{i+k})^2] = k\sigma^2\)





The lag-\(k\) difference telescopes into a sum of exactly \(k\) consecutive increments:
\[\theta_i - \theta_{i+k} = -(\xi_{i+1} + \cdots + \xi_{i+k})\]
Since the \(\xi_t\) are i.i.d. with mean 0 and variance \(\sigma^2\), squaring and taking expectations gives:
\[E[(\theta_i - \theta_{i+k})^2] = \sum_{s=i+1}^{i+k} \sum_{t=i+1}^{i+k} E[\xi_s \xi_t] = \sum_{s=i+1}^{i+k} \sigma^2 = k\sigma^2\]
where the cross terms \(E[\xi_s \xi_t] = 0\) for \(s \neq t\) by independence.
Summing over \(i = 1, \ldots, n-k\) (the valid pairs) then gives \(E[T_k] = (n-k)k\sigma^2\). For \(k \ll n\) this is approximately \(nk\sigma^2\), linear in \(k\).



so \(E[T_k(\theta,\theta)] = (n-k)k\sigma^2\), which is approximately linear in \(k\) for \(k \ll n\). Since the ECE is constructed to cancel exactly a linear trend in \(k \mapsto T_k\),
\[
E[\theta^T A \theta] = \frac{1}{2n}\bigl(2(n-1)\sigma^2 - 2(n-2)\sigma^2\bigr) = \frac{\sigma^2}{n} \to 0.
\]
The expected bias vanishes asymptotically — the ECE is nearly unbiased in expectation for random walk means, even though random walks are not piecewise constant.
Spectral interpretation. The power spectral density of a random walk concentrates at low frequencies: \(E[|\tilde{\theta}_j|^2] \propto 1/\sin^2(\pi j/n)\). Combined with \(\lambda_j \propto -\cos(2\pi j/n)\sin^2(\pi j/n)\), the expected bias is proportional to \(\sum_j \cos(2\pi j/n) = 0\), confirming the result.
Individual realizations. While \(E[\theta^T A \theta] \approx 0\), each realization of the random walk produces a nonzero bias. The distribution of realized biases has mean \(\approx \sigma^2/n\) and standard deviation that grows with \(\sigma^2\).

18.8 Linear Signals at Different Slopes
A natural conjecture is that steeper linear signals shift spectral energy to higher frequencies, producing more bias. The figures below test this: \(\theta_i = m \cdot (i/n - 0.5)\) for slopes \(m = 1, 2, 5, 10\).









The spectral shape is identical across all slopes — energy concentrates at low \(j\) in every case. What changes is only the scale: the bars grow as \(m^2\). Since \(\lambda_j \approx 0\) at those low frequencies, the bias remains small even for steep slopes. A linear signal is inherently low-frequency, and the ECE is insensitive to low-frequency structure by construction.

title: 20  Partial Correlation
text:
20.1 Motivation
The PC algorithm is a classical method for causal discovery. It recovers the skeleton of a causal graph by repeatedly testing conditional independence: an edge between \(X_i\) and \(X_j\) is removed whenever they are independent given some subset \(S\) of the remaining variables. For Gaussian data, conditional independence is equivalent to zero partial correlation, and the standard approach tests \(H_0: \rho_{ij \cdot S} = 0\) using a Fisher z-test on Pearson estimates.
This procedure fails when the time series have mean shifts. Simultaneous jumps in two series inflate the Pearson correlation between them, producing spurious edges in the estimated graph. The ECE addresses this: it estimates covariance from lagged differences, which cancel mean shifts algebraically and recover the true within-regime correlation.

title: 20  Partial Correlation
text:
20.2 Proposed Algorithm
We replace the Pearson-based partial correlation test in the PC algorithm with an ECE-based analogue. The procedure has three steps.
Step 1: Estimate the covariance matrix. Apply ece.cov to the \(n \times p\) data matrix to obtain \(\hat\Sigma\), a consistent estimator of the true covariance matrix under unknown mean shifts.
Step 2: Compute the partial correlation. For a given pair \((i, j)\) and conditioning set \(S\), extract the submatrix of \(\hat\Sigma\) indexed by \(\{i, j\} \cup S\) and apply the Schur complement: \[
\hat\rho_{ij \cdot S} = \frac{[\hat\Sigma_{ij \cdot S}]_{12}}{\sqrt{[\hat\Sigma_{ij \cdot S}]_{11} [\hat\Sigma_{ij \cdot S}]_{22}}}, \qquad \hat\Sigma_{ij \cdot S} = \hat\Sigma_{11} - \hat\Sigma_{12}\hat\Sigma_{22}^{-1}\hat\Sigma_{21}.
\]
Step 3: Bootstrap the standard error. The partial correlation is a nonlinear function of multiple entries of \(\hat\Sigma\), so its standard error cannot be read off directly. We use the parametric bootstrap: under \(H_0\), \(\bar S \sim N(0, V)\), where \(V\) is the bandwidth-2 variance estimator from the parametric bootstrap test. Each draw \(S^{(b)} \sim N(0, V)\) is a bootstrap replicate of \(\bar S\). Computing the partial correlation from each replicate gives the null distribution of \(\hat\rho_{ij \cdot S}\), and \(\widehat{SE} = \mathrm{SD}_b(\hat\rho^{(b)}_{ij \cdot S})\).
The test statistic \(z = \hat\rho_{ij \cdot S} / \widehat{SE}\) is referred to a standard normal, yielding a p-value for \(H_0: \rho_{ij \cdot S} = 0\).

title: 20  Partial Correlation
text:
20.3 Implementation

partial_cor_cov <- function(Sigma, i, j, cond = integer(0)) {
  idx <- c(i, j, cond)
  sub <- Sigma[idx, idx, drop = FALSE]
  if (length(cond) == 0)
    return(sub[1, 2] / sqrt(sub[1, 1] * sub[2, 2]))
  A <- sub[1:2, 1:2]
  B <- sub[1:2, -(1:2), drop = FALSE]
  C <- sub[-(1:2), -(1:2), drop = FALSE]
  schur <- A - B %*% solve(C) %*% t(B)
  schur[1, 2] / sqrt(schur[1, 1] * schur[2, 2])
}

ece.partial.test <- function(X, i, j, cond = integer(0), B = 500) {
  n <- nrow(X)
  p <- ncol(X)

  # Step 1: covariance estimate
  Sigma_hat <- ece.cov(X)

  # Step 2: partial correlation
  rho_hat <- partial_cor_cov(Sigma_hat, i, j, cond)

  # Step 3: bootstrap SE
  S_terms <- ece_terms(X)
  W <- (1 / n^2) * (
    t(S_terms) %*% S_terms +
    t(rotate(S_terms)) %*% S_terms + t(S_terms) %*% rotate(S_terms) +
    t(rotate(S_terms, 2)) %*% S_terms + t(S_terms) %*% rotate(S_terms, 2)
  )

  pairs <- combn(p, 2)

  bs_rhos <- map_dbl(1:B, ~ {
    S_b     <- MASS::mvrnorm(1, mu = rep(0, nrow(W)), Sigma = W)
    Sigma_b <- Sigma_hat
    for (k in seq_len(ncol(pairs))) {
      ii <- pairs[1, k]; jj <- pairs[2, k]
      Sigma_b[ii, jj] <- Sigma_b[jj, ii] <- S_b[k]
    }
    partial_cor_cov(Sigma_b, i, j, cond)
  })

  se_hat  <- sd(bs_rhos)
  z       <- rho_hat / se_hat
  p_value <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(z))

  list(estimate = rho_hat, se = se_hat, statistic = z, p.value = p_value)
}

section: A.2 SVD for Identifying the Null Space
text:
A.2 SVD for Identifying the Null Space
Given the constraint matrix \(G \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}\), the singular value decomposition is: \[G = U \Sigma V^T\] where \(U \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times m}\) and \(V \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}\) are orthogonal matrices, and \(\Sigma\) is a diagonal matrix with singular values \(\sigma_1 \geq \sigma_2 \geq \cdots \geq \sigma_{\min(m,n)} \geq 0\).

A.2.1 Connection to the Null Space
The null space of \(G\) is: \[\text{null}(G) = \{a \in \mathbb{R}^n : Ga = 0\}\]
If \(G\) has rank \(r < n\), the right singular vectors corresponding to zero singular values span the null space: \[\text{null}(G) = \text{span}\{v_{r+1}, v_{r+2}, \ldots, v_n\}\] where \(v_i\) are the columns of \(V\).


A.2.2 Steps to Identify the Null Space

Compute the SVD: \(G = U \Sigma V^T\)
Identify the rank \(r\) as the number of non-zero singular values
Extract the right singular vectors \(v_{r+1}, \ldots, v_n\) corresponding to the zero singular values
The null space basis is \(\text{null}(G) = \text{span}\{v_{r+1}, \ldots, v_n\}\)

title: Appendix A — Computational Solution
text:
A.3 Pseudoinverse and Min-Norm Solution
The Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse \(G^+\) is defined via SVD as: \[G^+ = V \Sigma^+ U^T\] where \(\Sigma^+\) is obtained by taking reciprocals of the non-zero singular values and transposing.
\(G^+\) simultaneously solves two optimality problems. When \(b \notin \text{col}(G)\) the system \(Ga = b\) is inconsistent, and \(G^+b\) is the least-squares solution minimizing \(\|Ga - b\|_2^2\). When the system is consistent but underdetermined, \(G^+b\) is the minimum-norm solution among all exact solutions.
For a system \(Ga = b\), the general solution is: \[a = G^+ b + \sum_{i=r+1}^{n} c_i v_i\] where the second term spans \(\text{null}(G)\). The norm of the general solution is: \[\|a\|^2 = \|G^+ b\|^2 + \sum_{i=r+1}^{n} c_i^2\] since \(G^+ b\) lies in the row space of \(G\), which is orthogonal to \(\text{null}(G)\). This is minimized by setting all \(c_i = 0\), giving the minimum-norm solution: \[a^* = G^+ b\]

title: Appendix B — Mean Removal
text:
B.1 Segmentation
Assume each time series has a piecewise-constant mean: \[X_t = \mu_t + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \mu_t \text{ piecewise constant.}\] Segmentation estimates \(\mu_t\) by the within-segment sample mean and subtracts it: \[\hat{\varepsilon}_t = X_t - \hat{\mu}_t.\] The residuals \(\hat{\varepsilon}_t\) are approximately stationary, so Pearson correlation applied to \((\hat{\varepsilon}_t^{(1)}, \hat{\varepsilon}_t^{(2)})\) estimates contemporaneous correlation between the two series.

title: Appendix B — Mean Removal
text:
B.2 Degrees of Freedom Correction
To do inference on Pearson correlation, we first estimate the correlation \(\hat{r}\). Then, we find that \[t_{\text{naive}} = \frac{r \sqrt{n-2}}{\sqrt{1-r^2}} \sim t_{n-2}.\] That is, the standard Pearson correlation has \(df = n-2\), because we use two degrees of freedom to estimate the mean and variance.
However, with segmentation, we must estimate multiple means. If there are \(K\) change points, then we must estimate \(K + 1\) sample means. In all, we must estimate \(K + 2\) parameters, so the correct statistic is \[t_{\text{correct}} = \frac{r\sqrt{n-K-2}}{\sqrt{1-r^2}} \sim t_{n-K-2}.\] Since both statistics share the same \(r\), they are related by \[t_{\text{naive}} = \lambda \cdot t_{\text{correct}}, \qquad \lambda = \sqrt{\frac{n-2}{n-K-2}} > 1.\]
The naive test rejects when \[|t_{\text{naive}}| > t_{n-2,\,\alpha/2}.\] Substituting \(t_{\text{naive}} = \lambda \cdot t_{\text{correct}}\), this is equivalent to \[|t_{\text{correct}}| > \frac{t_{n-2,\,\alpha/2}}{\lambda}.\] So the actual type I error of the naive test is \[P\!\left(|t_{\text{correct}}| > \frac{t_{n-2,\,\alpha/2}}{\lambda}\right), \qquad t_{\text{correct}} \sim t_{n-K-2}.\] Since \(\lambda > 1\), the threshold \(t_{n-2,\,\alpha/2}/\lambda < t_{n-K-2,\,\alpha/2}\), so the naive test rejects more often than it should.
Theoretical type I error. Given \(n\), \(K\), and \(\alpha\), the exact inflation is computable in closed form. Let \(c = t_{n-2,\,\alpha/2}\) be the naive critical value. The actual type I error is \[P\!\left(|T| > \frac{c}{\lambda}\right), \qquad T \sim t_{n-K-2}.\] In R: 2 * pt(-qt(1 - alpha/2, df = n-2) / lambda, df = n - K - 2).

title: Appendix C — Mathematical Background
text:
C.1 Expectation and Variance of Linear Transformations
For a random vector \(X\) and a fixed matrix \(A\):
\[
\mathbb{E}[AX] = A\,\mathbb{E}[X], \qquad \operatorname{Var}(AX) = A\operatorname{Var}(X)A^T.
\]
For a scalar linear form \(a^T X\), these specialize to
\[
\mathbb{E}[a^T X] = a^T \mathbb{E}[X], \qquad \operatorname{Var}(a^T X) = a^T \operatorname{Var}(X)\, a.
\]

title: Appendix C — Mathematical Background
section: C.2 Trace Trick for Quadratic Forms
text:
C.2 Trace Trick for Quadratic Forms
For any scalar \(z\), \(z = \operatorname{tr}(z)\). So for vectors \(u, v\) and a fixed matrix \(A\),
\[
u^T A v = \operatorname{tr}(u^T A v).
\]
Applying the cyclic property of trace, \(\operatorname{tr}(u^T A v) = \operatorname{tr}(A v u^T)\). Taking expectations and using linearity,
\[
\mathbb{E}[u^T A v] = \operatorname{tr}\!\left(A\,\mathbb{E}[v u^T]\right).
\]
In particular, if \(u = \varepsilon_x\) and \(v = \varepsilon_y\) with cross-covariance \(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_y \varepsilon_x^T] = \Sigma_{xy}\), then
\[
\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_x^T A \varepsilon_y] = \operatorname{tr}(A \Sigma_{xy}).
\]

title: Appendix C — Mathematical Background
text:
C.3 Properties of Circulant Matrices
Let \(C_1 = \operatorname{circ}(0, 1, 0, \ldots, 0)\) be the elementary shift-by-one matrix, so \(C_1^k = C_k\). The following facts hold:

Power. \(C_k = C_1^k\), so applying a shift of \(k\) is the same as applying a shift of 1 exactly \(k\) times. As a consequence, every circulant matrix is a polynomial in \(C_1\): \(\operatorname{circ}(a_0, \ldots, a_{n-1}) = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k C_1^k\).
Transpose. \(C_k^T = C_{n-k} = C_k^{-1}\), since \(C_k\) is a permutation matrix.
Circulant form. \(C_k = \operatorname{circ}(e_k)\), where \(e_k\) is the standard basis vector with a 1 in position \(k\) and 0s elsewhere. That is, \(C_k\) is the circulant matrix whose first row has a single 1 on the \(k\)-th band.

title: Appendix C — Mathematical Background
section: C.4 Spectral Properties of Circulant Matrices
text:
C.4 Spectral Properties of Circulant Matrices
Every circulant matrix \(A = \operatorname{circ}(a_0, \ldots, a_{n-1})\) is diagonalized by the DFT matrix \(F\),
\[
A = F^* \Lambda F, \qquad F_{jk} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\,\omega^{jk}, \quad \omega = e^{-2\pi i/n},
\]
where indices \(j, k\) run from \(0\) to \(n-1\). Since \(F\) is unitary (\(FF^* = I\)), this is the eigendecomposition \(A = Q\Lambda Q^{-1}\) with \(Q = F^*\).
Eigenvalues. The \(j\)-th eigenvalue is the DFT of the first row evaluated at frequency \(j\):
\[
\lambda_j = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k\,\omega^{jk}.
\]
Eigenvectors. The columns of \(Q = F^*\) are the eigenvectors. The \(j\)-th eigenvector is
\[
q_j = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\bigl(1,\, \omega^{-j},\, \omega^{-2j},\, \ldots,\, \omega^{-(n-1)j}\bigr)^T,
\]
a complex sinusoid at frequency \(j/n\).
Real symmetric case. When \(A\) is real and symmetric (i.e. \(a_k = a_{n-k}\)), the eigenvalues are real and come in symmetric pairs: \(\lambda_j = \lambda_{n-j}\).

title: Appendix C — Mathematical Background
section: C.5 Variance of a Product of Correlated Standard Normals
text:
C.5 Variance of a Product of Correlated Standard Normals
Let \((z_x, z_y)\) be a standard bivariate Gaussian with zero mean, unit variances, and correlation \(\rho\). Then
\[
\operatorname{Var}(z_x z_y) = 1 + \rho^2.
\]
Proof. Decompose \(z_y = \rho z_x + \sqrt{1 - \rho^2}\, w\) where \(w \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\) is independent of \(z_x\). Then
\[
z_x z_y = \rho z_x^2 + \sqrt{1 - \rho^2}\, z_x w.
\]
Since \(z_x \perp w\), the two terms are independent, so their variances add:
\[
\operatorname{Var}(z_x z_y) = \rho^2 \operatorname{Var}(z_x^2) + (1 - \rho^2)\operatorname{Var}(z_x w).
\]
For \(z_x \sim \mathcal{N}(0,1)\): \(\operatorname{Var}(z_x^2) = \mathbb{E}[z_x^4] - (\mathbb{E}[z_x^2])^2 = 3 - 1 = 2\). For independent standard normals: \(\operatorname{Var}(z_x w) = \mathbb{E}[z_x^2]\mathbb{E}[w^2] = 1\). Therefore,
\[
\operatorname{Var}(z_x z_y) = 2\rho^2 + (1 - \rho^2) = 1 + \rho^2. \qquad \square
\]

title: Appendix D — Other Mathematical Results
text:
D.1 Properties of \(A^2\)
Let \(A\) be a symmetric circulant with first row \((a_0, a_1, \ldots, a_{n-1})\) and eigenvalues \(\lambda_0, \ldots, \lambda_{n-1}\).
Structure. Since the product of two circulants is circulant and \((A^2)^T = (A^T)^2 = A^2\), \(A^2\) is also a symmetric circulant. Its first row has \(j\)-th entry given by the autocorrelation
\[
(A^2)_j = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k\, a_{j - k \bmod n}.
\]
Positive semidefiniteness. For any vector \(x\), \(x^T A^2 x = \|Ax\|^2 \geq 0\), so \(A^2 \succeq 0\).
Eigenvalues. The eigenvalues of \(A^2\) are \(\lambda_k^2\), so
\[
\operatorname{tr}(A^2) = \sum_k \lambda_k^2 = \|A\|_F^2.
\]
Explicit trace formula. Since every row of a circulant is a cyclic permutation of the first row, each row has the same squared norm, giving
\[
\operatorname{tr}(A^2) = \|A\|_F^2 = n \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k^2 = n\!\left(a_0^2 + 2\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor} a_k^2\right),
\]
where the last equality uses the symmetry \(a_k = a_{n-k}\).

title: Appendix D — Other Mathematical Results
text:
D.2 Lower Bound on \(\operatorname{tr}(A^2)\)
Since \(\operatorname{tr}(A) = \sum_i \lambda_i = 1\) and \(\operatorname{tr}(A^2) = \sum_i \lambda_i^2\), Jensen’s inequality gives
\[
\operatorname{tr}(A^2) = \sum_i \lambda_i^2 \geq \frac{\left(\sum_i \lambda_i\right)^2}{n} = \frac{1}{n},
\]
with equality when all eigenvalues are equal. Thus the noise contribution \((\sigma_x^2\sigma_y^2 + \sigma_{xy}^2)\operatorname{tr}(A^2) = O(1/n)\), which shows the estimator is consistent.

title: Appendix D — Other Mathematical Results
text:
D.3 Closed Form of \((K^TK)^{-1}K^T\)
The design matrix is \(K \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times 2}\) with \(K_{k,1} = 1\) and \(K_{k,2} = k\) for \(k = 1, \ldots, L\). We use the Gaussian sum identities
\[\sum_{k=1}^L 1 = L, \qquad \sum_{k=1}^L k = \frac{L(L+1)}{2}, \qquad \sum_{k=1}^L k^2 = \frac{L(L+1)(2L+1)}{6}.\]
Step 1: Compute \(K^TK\).
\[K^TK = \begin{bmatrix} L & \dfrac{L(L+1)}{2} \\[6pt] \dfrac{L(L+1)}{2} & \dfrac{L(L+1)(2L+1)}{6} \end{bmatrix}.\]
Step 2: Compute \(\det(K^TK)\).
\[\det(K^TK) = \frac{L^2(L+1)(2L+1)}{6} - \frac{L^2(L+1)^2}{4} = L^2(L+1)\cdot\frac{2(2L+1) - 3(L+1)}{12} = \frac{L^2(L^2-1)}{12}.\]
Step 3: Invert \(K^TK\).
Applying the \(2\times 2\) inverse formula and simplifying,
\[
(K^TK)^{-1} = \frac{12}{L^2(L^2-1)}\begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{L(L+1)(2L+1)}{6} & -\dfrac{L(L+1)}{2} \\[6pt] -\dfrac{L(L+1)}{2} & L \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2(2L+1)}{L(L-1)} & \dfrac{-6}{L(L-1)} \\[6pt] \dfrac{-6}{L(L-1)} & \dfrac{12}{L(L-1)(L+1)} \end{bmatrix}.
\]
Step 4: Multiply by \(K^T\).
The \(j\)-th column of \((K^TK)^{-1}K^T\) is \((K^TK)^{-1}(1,j)^T\). Computing each row,
\[
\bigl((K^TK)^{-1}K^T\bigr)_{1,j} = \frac{2(2L+1)}{L(L-1)} - \frac{6j}{L(L-1)} = \frac{2(2L+1-3j)}{L(L-1)},
\] \[
\bigl((K^TK)^{-1}K^T\bigr)_{2,j} = \frac{-6}{L(L-1)} + \frac{12j}{L(L-1)(L+1)} = \frac{6(2j - L - 1)}{L(L-1)(L+1)}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
(K^TK)^{-1}K^T = \frac{1}{L(L-1)}\begin{bmatrix} 2(2L+1-3j) \\[4pt] \dfrac{6(2j-L-1)}{L+1} \end{bmatrix}_{j=1}^{L}.
\]
Since \(H = \frac{1}{2n}(K^TK)^{-1}K^T\), the first row is
\[H_{1,j} = \frac{2L+1-3j}{nL(L-1)},\]
which is linear in \(j\).
